fields.text:
• When describing observations, link them directly to clinical reasoning and a
cooperative next step.
•
“Joan appears stable on her current antipsychotic regimen. A GP review of
ongoing need may be appropriate given current stability.”
•
“Pain is well controlled. A gradual reduction in opioid dose may be suitable if
comfort is maintained.”
•
“If sedation continues, the GP may consider switching to a less sedating
alternative.”
•
“Indication not clearly documented — GP to confirm and continue if benefits
outweigh risks.”
•
“Monitoring progress will guide whether rationalisation or deprescribing is
warranted.”
• These sentences move from observation → interpretation → collaborative
action without sounding directive.

• When you need to suggest an action, phrase it so that it sounds collegial:
•
Instead of “consider…”, say “it may be appropriate to…” or “a review of [X]
could be beneficial.”
•
Instead of “recommend…”, use “it is reasonable to suggest…” or “GP might be
advised to…”
•
Instead of “may benefit from…”, try “could respond well to…” or “likely to
experience improvement if…”
•
Instead of “please monitor or review…”, use “monitor for changes and adjust
as clinically appropriate.”
•
Instead of “cease…”, write “discontinue if no ongoing benefit or if indication
not confirmed.”
•
Instead of “should…” or “needs to…”, use “it may be reasonable to…” or
“would benefit from…”
• These forms keep your tone advisory rather than commanding while
maintaining clinical authority.

• Some expressions weaken or over-personalise reports. Replace them with
neutral, outcome-based language.
•
Avoid saying “stop this medication”; use “cease if no longer indicated.”
•
Avoid “GP must review immediately”; instead say “GP review is strongly
advised due to identified risk.”
•
Replace “patient refuses to comply” with “resident declined treatment after
discussion.”
•
Replace “non-compliant” with “non-adherent” or “not tolerating therapy.”
•
Replace “failed therapy” with “did not achieve desired response.”
• Each revision keeps focus on the medication or outcome, not on blame or
authority.

• A simple structure for professional phrasing:
• Observation → Interpretation → Collaborative Action
• Example:
• “Sedation noted with evening quetiapine. This may contribute to daytime
lethargy. GP may consider dose timing adjustment or alternative agent if
symptoms persist.”

• “Ongoing review may guide next steps.”
• “Monitor response and adjust if clinically appropriate.”
• “Follow-up results will determine need for continuation.”
• “Reassess benefit versus risk at the next GP visit.”
• “Continue monitoring for improvement or adverse effects.”
• “GP may wish to review progress at regular intervals.”

• “A gradual dose reduction may be appropriate if stable.”
• “Up-titration could be considered if symptoms remain uncontrolled.”
• “Dose adjustment may improve tolerability.”
• “Review current dose for potential simplification.”
• “If well-controlled, step down to the lowest effective dose.”

• “Cease if no ongoing indication or measurable benefit.”
• “Deprescribing may be reasonable if symptoms have resolved.”
• “Trial reduction could clarify ongoing need.”
• “Simplifying therapy may reduce risk of adverse effects.”
• “If discontinued, monitor for recurrence of symptoms.”
• “Gradual taper recommended to minimise withdrawal effects.”

• “Behaviour appears settled on current regimen.”
• “Review psychotropic need if no recent behavioural incidents.”
• “If BPSD remains stable, consider gradual dose reduction.”
• “Continue only if clear evidence of benefit and consent documented.”
• “Ensure restraint register and consent are current.”
• “If sedation persists, GP may consider less sedating alternative.”

• “Pain appears well controlled on current regimen.”
• “Trial dose reduction may be suitable if comfort maintained.”
• “Review PRN use for potential conversion to regular dosing or cessation.”
• “If ongoing pain, assess non-pharmacological strategies.”
• “Continue bowel regimen to prevent opioid-induced constipation.”

• “Indication not clearly documented — GP to confirm ongoing need.”
• “Review chart to ensure indication and duration recorded.”
• “Confirm therapeutic intent before continuation.”
• “Cease if no corresponding diagnosis or monitoring plan.”
• “Clarifying indication may support deprescribing.”

• “Sedation likely contributing to daytime fatigue.”
• “Observed confusion may relate to anticholinergic load.”
• “Dizziness possibly linked to antihypertensive combination.”
• “Low mood may reflect medication effect rather than condition relapse.”
• “Weight loss noted; review for appetite-suppressing agents.”

• “Staff reminded to document indication and outcome after PRN use.”
• “Reinforce correct administration and timing with nursing team.”
• “Provide education on swallowing safety and formulation changes.”
• “Ensure residents and staff aware of potential side-effects.”
• “Reinforce importance of hydration and regular observation.”

When in doubt, soften instructions by using:
• “It may be appropriate to…”
• “It is reasonable to suggest…”
• “GP may wish to consider…”
• “Review could be beneficial if clinically indicated.”
• “Continue monitoring and adjust as required.”
Avoid using absolute or directive language such as must, needs to, or should unless
citing a legal or regulatory requirement.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Hyperkalaemia, renal function decline, and postural hypotension—especially in
combination therapy.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check eGFR and K⁺ at baseline, 1–2 weeks after changes, then 3–6-monthly.
Reduce or cease if K⁺ > 5.5 mmol/L or eGFR falls > 25%.
Avoid triple therapy (ACEI + ARB + Spiro).

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for secretion control in palliative care.
Less central sedation than hyoscine hydrobromide, but can still cause dry mouth,
constipation, urinary retention, and tachycardia.
May be used unnecessarily in the final hours, causing distressing dryness or
restlessness.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use for excessive respiratory secretions (“death rattle”) only when non-
pharmacological measures fail.
Typical dose: 200–400 micrograms SC q4h PRN (via syringe driver 600–1,200
micrograms/24 h).
Avoid if minimal secretions or when comfort not improved.
Reassess every 4–6 hours; cease if no benefit.
Ensure oral care and gentle suctioning are optimised before initiation.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for colicky abdominal pain, bowel obstruction, or respiratory secretions in end-
of-life care.
Can cause dry mouth, urinary retention, tachycardia, and confusion in frail residents.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use 10–20 mg SC q4h PRN or continuous infusion 40–120 mg/24 h if symptoms
persist.
Avoid if severe urinary retention, glaucoma, or tachyarrhythmia.
If no response after two doses, reassess cause and consider glycopyrrolate instead.
Review effect on comfort regularly; cease if secretions or spasm resolved.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for anxiety, agitation, or dyspnoea at end of life.
Risk of oversedation, respiratory depression, and paradoxical agitation if titrated too
quickly.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Start 1–2.5 mg SC q1h PRN; repeat every 30–60 minutes if distress continues.
For syringe driver: 10–30 mg/24 h (individualised).
Review sedation depth and respiratory rate at least every 2 hours initially.
Combine with opioid if dyspnoea predominant; otherwise use alone for agitation.
Stop or reduce dose if excessive sedation or noisy breathing develops.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Effective for agitation, delirium, or nausea in palliative care but may cause
extrapyramidal effects, sedation, and QT prolongation.
Caution in Parkinson’s disease or Lewy body dementia.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Start 0.5–1 mg SC or PO q1–2h PRN, max 5 mg/24 h; continuous infusion 2–5 mg/24
h if persistent symptoms.
Monitor for rigidity, tremor, or oversedation.
Avoid combination with other antipsychotics unless directed by palliative specialist.
If Parkinsonian features, use olanzapine or quetiapine instead.
Review benefit daily; cease once agitation or nausea settles.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Palliative Care | NSW Health End-of-Life Medicines Guidance

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Commonly prescribed for hypertension or benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). In
older adults, these agents can cause marked postural hypotension, dizziness,
syncope, and falls, especially at night or when combined with other
antihypertensives.
Often continued for years without clear BP benefit or BPH indication.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Review indication—if used solely for hypertension, consider switch to ACEI, ARB, or
calcium-channel blocker.
For BPH, use tamsulosin or alfuzosin (uroselective) to reduce systemic hypotension
risk.
Check standing and sitting BP weekly for 2–4 weeks after initiation or dose change.
Cease gradually (halve dose for 1–2 weeks) to avoid rebound hypertension.
Document orthostatic BP trend in care plan and review after any fall.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Occasionally charted for resistant hypertension, agitation, or menopausal flushing.
High risk of rebound hypertension on abrupt cessation and CNS effects (drowsiness,
confusion, dry mouth, constipation).
In aged care, clonidine often persists long after initial indication resolved.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication and duration; avoid as chronic therapy where possible.
If discontinuing, taper slowly over 2–4 weeks to prevent rebound hypertension.
Monitor BP and heart rate closely during taper.
If used for behavioural symptoms, consider alternative non-sedating agents or non-
drug strategies.
For resistant hypertension, seek specialist input for substitution (e.g. moxonidine or
hydralazine).

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Cardiovascular | RACGP Falls & Medication Safety

entries.title: Biologic Therapy for Severe Asthma / COPD (e.g. Mepolizumab, Benralizumab, Dupilumab)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for severe eosinophilic asthma or Type-2 inflammatory disease when inhaled
triple therapy (ICS/LABA/LAMA) is inadequate.
Not indicated for mild or moderate COPD unless eosinophilic phenotype confirmed.
High cost, injection-site reactions, and logistical issues (cold chain, nurse
administration) limit aged-care practicality.
Residents may remain on biologic therapy after hospital initiation without ongoing
review.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication, eosinophil count, and ongoing specialist follow-up.
Ensure inhaler adherence and technique are optimised before initiation or
continuation.
Store pens/syringes refrigerated; rotate injection sites.
If resident is clinically stable with no exacerbations for >12 months, review need with
respiratory specialist.
Do not initiate or continue biologic therapy in RACF without clear documentation of
diagnosis and review schedule.
Document last injection date, dose, and next due date on medication chart.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text:
PBS Criteria for Severe Eosinophilic Asthma | eTG Respiratory | TSANZ Biologic
Therapies Guidance

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Home or facility oxygen often continued indefinitely without reassessment.
Incorrect flow rates or unnecessary oxygen in CO₂ retainers (COPD) may cause
hypercapnia, drowsiness, or acidosis.
Safety risks include fire hazard (especially near smokers or open flames).

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication with recent SpO₂ or arterial blood gas:
– Chronic hypoxaemia: SpO₂ ≤ 88 % (or ≤ 90 % with cor pulmonale).
– Target saturation: 88–92 % for COPD; 92–96 % for others.
Review prescription at least every 3–6 months or after clinical change.
Ensure equipment maintenance, humidifier hygiene, and clear signage (“No
Smoking – Oxygen in Use”).
For short-term or palliative comfort use, document goal of care (comfort vs
correction).
Cease long-term oxygen if resting SpO₂ > 92 % on room air over multiple readings.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text:
AMH | eTG Respiratory | Thoracic Society of Australia & New Zealand (TSANZ)
Oxygen Therapy Guidelines

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Adjuncts to levodopa for “wearing-off,” but may cause insomnia, orthostatic
hypotension, nausea, hallucinations—risk higher in frailty/cognitive impairment.
Important interactions: risk of serotonin syndrome with SSRIs/SNRIs, mirtazapine,
tramadol, dextromethorphan; hypertensive reactions with certain sympathomimetics.
Dietary tyramine restriction usually not required at standard PD doses, but caution
with concentrated tyramine foods.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm goal (reduce “off” time) and document functional benefit (mobility, ADLs).
If hallucinations, agitation, or falls emerge, consider dose reduction or trial
withdrawal (step down MAO-B before changing levodopa).
Avoid or review if on serotonergic antidepressants or tramadol—seek prescriber
plan (staggered washout if switching).
For selegiline: avoid evening dosing (metabolites → insomnia).
For rasagiline: check hepatic function; avoid moderate–severe impairment.
Monitor BP sitting/standing, sleep, mood, and falls within 2–4 weeks of changes.
Reassess every 3–6 months; cease if no clear benefit or adverse effects persist.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Neurology / Parkinson’s disease

entries.title: Calcitriol and Alfacalcidol (Active Vitamin D Analogues)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and hypoparathyroidism to manage
hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
Overuse or duplicate charting with standard Vitamin D can cause hypercalcaemia,
confusion, constipation, and cardiac arrhythmia.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication (renal osteodystrophy vs osteoporosis prevention).
Avoid concurrent use with cholecalciferol unless specifically directed by
nephrologist.
Monitor Ca²⁺ and phosphate every 3–6 months; stop or reduce dose if
hypercalcaemia develops.
Typical maintenance: Calcitriol 0.25–0.5 microg daily.
Document prescriber (nephrology) and review schedule clearly.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for IBS-type cramp or colic; anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation,
urinary retention, confusion) problematic in frail residents.
Often continued long-term without symptom diary or clear benefit.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm functional benefit (pain episodes ↓, stool normalised).
Prefer short trials (2–4 weeks) with stop date; cease if no improvement.
Avoid in glaucoma, urinary retention, severe constipation, or high ACB score.
Optimise non-drug measures: small low-FODMAP trials, fibre titration, peppermint
oil, fluids.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Gastroenterology

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Indicated for cholestatic liver disease (e.g., PBC); sometimes continued for
asymptomatic gallstones or fatty liver without evidence.
May cause diarrhoea; benefit requires months of use and LFT monitoring.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Verify indication with recent diagnosis and LFTs; avoid for simple gallstones/NAFLD
without specialist advice.
Monitor ALP, GGT, ALT every 3–6 months; continue only if biochemical or
symptomatic response.
Stop if no objective improvement after 6–12 months or adverse effects occur.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Hepatology

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Recurrent confusion and falls may reflect encephalopathy; under- or over-treating
can cause dehydration, diarrhoea, electrolyte imbalance.
Rifaximin often added without reassessing lactulose dosing or bowel chart.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Target 2–3 soft stools/day with lactulose (common start: 15–30 mL BD–TDS; titrate
to effect).
Add rifaximin 550 mg BD for recurrent episodes despite optimal lactulose.
Monitor hydration, Na⁺/K⁺, and bowel chart; reduce dose if diarrhoea.
Investigate precipitants (infection, GI bleed, sedatives, dehydration).
Educate staff on stool targets; document review date and triggers for GP
notification.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Hepatology | Cirrhosis Care guidance

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Common empiric antibiotics in RACFs; often continued beyond intended duration
(e.g., “infection resolved but still on chart”).
Frequent duplication with broader agents (e.g., cephalexin + amoxicillin/clavulanate).
Long-term use promotes C. difficile infection, resistance, and microbiome disruption.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Always confirm indication, start date, and intended duration (typically 5–7 days for
skin or urinary infections).
If infection resolved or no documented diagnosis—cease or mark review date
clearly.
Avoid “chronic prophylaxis” unless under urology or infectious diseases guidance.
For cellulitis, prefer flucloxacillin; for UTI, check culture results before repeat
prescribing.
Audit all residents on antibiotics >7 days and escalate to GP for review.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: eTG Antibiotic | AURA Antimicrobial Stewardship | AMH

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for recurrent UTI prophylaxis, but efficacy depends on acidic urine (pH < 6)
and adequate renal function.
Often continued indefinitely without review or urine pH monitoring.
Ineffective if on alkaline agents (e.g., antacids, urinary alkalinisers).

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication (≥3 UTIs/year despite hygiene and hydration optimisation).
Ensure urine pH monitoring—consider adjunct vitamin C to maintain acidity.
Avoid if eGFR < 30 mL/min, or with indwelling catheters (limited benefit).
Cease if infection-free for ≥6 months or adverse effects (dysuria, rash).
Reassess every 3–6 months; document review outcome.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG UTI | RACGP Antimicrobial Stewardship Guidance

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
5-α reductase inhibitor used for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) or male pattern
hair loss.
In aged-care males, often continued despite minimal urinary benefit or after
catheterisation.
Can cause sexual dysfunction, depression, and falsely low PSA levels.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm ongoing BPH symptoms (frequency, hesitancy, retention) before continuing.
If catheterised or on combination therapy (e.g. with tamsulosin), reassess need every
6–12 months.
Explain that PSA will be reduced by ~50%; interpret results accordingly.
Cease if no benefit after 6–12 months or if adverse effects (low mood, fatigue) occur.
Avoid for alopecia in frail elderly—benefit minimal, risk greater.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for nocturia, nocturnal enuresis, or diabetes insipidus.
Risk of hyponatraemia, confusion, seizures, and fluid overload—especially in elderly
or renal impairment.
Frequently continued without sodium monitoring or clear indication.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication and review other reversible causes (diuretics timing, CHF,
diabetes).
Check Na⁺ at baseline, within 3–7 days of initiation, and monthly for 3 months, then
quarterly.
Cease immediately if Na⁺ < 130 mmol/L or new confusion/lethargy.
For nocturia: use lowest effective dose (e.g. 25 µg oral lyophilisate or 60 µg tablet at
bedtime).
Avoid in eGFR < 50 mL/min or uncontrolled heart failure.
Educate staff on strict fluid restriction overnight.
Reassess efficacy and sodium every review cycle.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Urology | Therapeutic Guidelines – Diabetes Insipidus & Nocturia

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Commonly charted for pressure injuries or post-surgery recovery, but often
continued indefinitely after wounds heal.
High-dose or prolonged zinc can cause nausea, reduced copper absorption, and
anaemia.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use zinc sulfate 220 mg daily (≈50 mg elemental) short-term — stop after 8–12
weeks or once wound healed.
Combine with Vitamin C 500–1000 mg daily for collagen synthesis if dietary intake
low.
Avoid chronic use without re-evaluation or if serum zinc normal.
Encourage protein intake, hydration, and turning schedule as core wound care
measures.
Reassess all supplements at monthly wound review.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
High-protein, arginine-based formulas used to promote wound healing.
Can be duplicated with standard oral nutrition supplements, leading to excess
protein or calorie load.
Benefit diminishes once wounds close or protein intake adequate.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use under dietitian guidance only for Stage 3–4 pressure injuries or post-surgical
wounds.
Review after 4–6 weeks; discontinue if wound healing complete or intake sufficient
from diet.
Avoid combining with standard oral supplements unless directed.
Document start and expected review date on care plan.
Reinforce repositioning, hydration, and pressure off-loading as first-line.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: RACGP Wound Care | NHMRC Pressure Injury Prevention | AMH

entries.title: Opioid Use in Renal Impairment (Switching to Fentanyl or Hydromorphone)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Morphine and oxycodone depend on renal clearance. In residents with eGFR < 30
mL/min, active metabolites can accumulate, causing sedation, confusion,
hallucinations, myoclonus, and respiratory depression.
Opioid toxicity is often mistaken for pain escalation, leading to inappropriate dose
increases.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Monitor eGFR and clinical response regularly in all residents on opioids.
If eGFR < 30 mL/min, or signs of neurotoxicity develop, consider conversion to a
non-renally cleared opioid:
• Fentanyl: Preferred when pain is stable and oral intake poor. Start with 12–25
µg/h patch (≈30–60 mg oral morphine/24 h) or 12.5–25 µg SC q1h PRN,
titrate slowly. Avoid in opioid-naïve residents.
• Hydromorphone: Preferred for titration when renal impairment present. Start
0.25–0.5 mg SC q1h PRN or 2–4 mg/24 h syringe driver, titrate to comfort.
Avoid codeine, tramadol, tapentadol, and long-acting morphine/oxycodone
in renal impairment.
Document conversion, monitor sedation, and review effect within 24 hours.
If comfortable and stable on small doses of oral oxycodone, maintain
temporarily (<30 mg oMEDD) with close review and plan to switch as renal
function declines.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Palliative Care | Australian Renal Supportive Care Guidelines

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Dose often unchanged for years; absorption reduced by calcium, iron, or food.
Over-replacement may cause atrial fibrillation or bone loss in older adults.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Review indication and latest TSH every 6–12 months.
Administer on an empty stomach; separate from Ca/Fe supplements by ≥4 h.
If TSH suppressed (<0.4 mIU/L), consider 25–50 µg reduction.
Liothyronine use in RACFs is rarely required—verify specialist intent.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Endocrine | RACGP

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Long-term use (>5 years bisphosphonates or >7 months delay in Denosumab)
increases risk of atypical fracture or rebound vertebral fracture.
Dental extractions without precaution may cause jaw necrosis.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Review therapy duration annually.
Consider “drug holiday” if BMD stable ≥5 years on oral bisphosphonates.
Do not delay Denosumab doses >7 months; if stopping, give oral bisphosphonate
cover.
Encourage Ca/Vit D repletion and dental check before initiation.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | Therapeutic Guidelines | RACGP Osteoporosis

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Often charted for “malnutrition” without clear duration. Deficiency risk higher with
alcohol intake, malabsorption, or poor oral intake.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Short-term use (100 mg daily for 1–3 months) for repletion.
Continue only if ongoing malnutrition or alcohol use present.
Combine with multivitamin; review need quarterly.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | NHMRC Malnutrition Guidelines

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Chronic use (>3 weeks) suppresses adrenal axis; abrupt cessation can cause adrenal
crisis.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If >3 weeks of therapy or >7.5 mg/day, taper by 2.5–5 mg every 1–2 weeks
depending on indication.
If long-term, consider morning dosing and bone protection (Ca/Vit D ±
bisphosphonate).
Monitor BP, glucose, mood, infection risk.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: eTG | AMH | RACGP

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Continuation despite very low LDL (<1 mmol/L) or limited life expectancy.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
For primary prevention: cease if >75 years, frail, or LDL <1 mmol/L.
For secondary prevention: consider halving dose (Atorvastatin 40 → 20 → 10 mg).
Repeat LFTs and lipid profile at 3–6 months post change.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | RACGP Lipid Management

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Dual diuretic therapy may cause dehydration, hypotension, and severe
hypokalaemia.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Reserve for resistant oedema only under GP supervision.
Monitor BP, weight, Cr, Na, K every 1–2 weeks after change.
Add K+ supplement or ACEI if needed; review indication monthly.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Cardiovascular

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used when BP uncontrolled on triple therapy; high risk of postural hypotension,
dizziness.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check for duplication with clonidine or alpha-blockers.
Start low (Hydralazine 12.5 mg BD or Moxonidine 200 µg daily) and titrate slowly.
Avoid in frailty or orthostatic hypotension; monitor BP sitting and standing.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: eTG Hypertension | AMH

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Switching due to renal decline or interaction often poorly documented; overlap risks
bleed or clot.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
When switching to warfarin: start both, stop DOAC once INR ≥2.0.
When switching to DOAC: stop warfarin, start DOAC once INR <2.0.
Check renal function before any change; document indication clearly.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: eTG Anticoagulation | AMH

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Both risk hyperkalaemia, especially with ACEI/ARB or renal impairment. Eplerenone
preferred if gynecomastia occurs.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check K+ and eGFR within 1 week of start, then monthly x3.
Cease or reduce if K+ >5.0 mmol/L or eGFR <30 mL/min.
Avoid duplication; use one MRA only.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | Heart Failure Guidelines

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Often continued chronically without proven benefit; can worsen cough or nausea.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Trial for 2–4 weeks only in productive COPD/bronchiectasis.
Cease if ineffective.
Encourage hydration and airway clearance physiotherapy.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | COPD-X

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for sputum clearance; may cause bronchospasm if not pre-treated with
bronchodilator.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use 4–6 mL of 3–7% saline via nebuliser, preceded by bronchodilator.
Cease if excessive cough or discomfort.
Review every 3 months; ensure device hygiene.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: COPD-X | TSANZ

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Long-term oral prednisone for COPD often continued unnecessarily.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Gradually taper by 2.5 mg every 1–2 weeks if stable.
Switch to inhaled corticosteroid maintenance if indicated.
Monitor BGL, mood, and infection signs.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: eTG Respiratory | COPD-X

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Concurrent tiotropium + umeclidinium or indacaterol + vilanterol causes duplication
and dry mouth.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Ensure single LAMA or LABA per regimen.
Rationalise to combination inhaler if possible (e.g., Spiolto , Ultibro ).
Educate staff on device differentiation.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: COPD-X | AMH

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Levetiracetam and phenytoin often continued despite no seizures for years.
Dose may be inappropriate in renal/hepatic impairment.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If seizure-free >2 years, discuss neurologist-led taper.
Check Na⁺ (carbamazepine), LFTs (valproate, phenytoin), eGFR (levetiracetam).
Avoid multiple anticonvulsants unless active seizure disorder.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Neurology

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Used long-term for neuropathic pain or insomnia; high anticholinergic load, falls risk.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If ineffective, reduce by 10–25% every 1–2 weeks.
Avoid in dementia or high ACB score (>3).
Consider duloxetine or pregabalin if neuropathic.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Pain

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Combining SSRI + SNRI or TCA ↑ serotonin toxicity risk.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Rationalise to single effective agent; taper one over 2–4 weeks.
Monitor for serotonin syndrome (sweating, tremor, agitation).
Avoid fluoxetine overlap (long half-life).

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Psychiatry

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Clozapine may be continued during electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) but requires
monitoring for hypotension and seizures.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Ensure psychiatrist-led oversight.
Check FBC weekly x6 months, then monthly.
Hold dose on morning of ECT; restart post-treatment.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: Clozapine Titration Guideline | RANZCP

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Potent long-acting opioid with complex kinetics; accumulation risk in renal/liver
impairment.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Initiate only under palliative or pain specialist.
Start 2.5 mg PO q8–12h; titrate no more than every 5–7 days.
Avoid PRN use; ensure ECG monitoring (QTc).

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: eTG Palliative | AMH

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Low-dose SC or oral ketamine used for refractory pain; hallucinations and confusion
possible.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Reserve for specialist initiation.
Start 10–25 mg SC q4–6h PRN or 100 mg/24 h infusion if directed.
Monitor mental state; cease if agitation develops.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: eTG Palliative Care | NSW Health

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Dual use increases QT prolongation, dystonia risk.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use one only.
Limit metoclopramide to ≤5 days unless palliative.
If domperidone, review ECG annually.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG GI

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Continued despite improved digestion or uncertain indication.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use for confirmed pancreatic insufficiency only.
Dose 25,000–40,000 units lipase/meal.
Cease trial if no benefit after 2 weeks.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | Pancreatic Disorders

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Prolonged use → constipation, QT prolongation.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Limit to ≤5 days unless palliative.
Monitor bowel function; add laxative if regular use needed.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Oncology

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Constipation from regular opioids often undertreated; risk of impaction and
delirium.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Start stimulant + osmotic laxative routinely.
Avoid PRN-only bowel regimens.
Monitor stool chart daily in palliative or opioid use.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: eTG Palliative | AMH

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Unnecessary continuation after anaemia resolved; constipation common.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check Hb/ferritin 6–8 weeks post-initiation.
Cease when ferritin >100 µg/L or Hb normal.
Use alternate-day dosing to reduce GI upset.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Anaemia

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Often co-charted unnecessarily; may mask B12 deficiency.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check B12 before folate.
Continue folate only if dietary deficiency or methotrexate therapy.
Cease once corrected.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Haematology

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Bottles reused beyond 3 months; contamination risk.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Replace preservative-free products every 3 months.
Label open date; store below 25°C.
Ensure correct technique (no-touch tip).

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | Ophthalmology

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Reinfestation from contacts or bedding common.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Treat all close contacts concurrently.
Wash bedding/clothing in hot water and dry on high heat.
Repeat after 7 days if needed.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: eTG Infection Control | CDC

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Used for herpes labialis; little benefit after vesicle crusting.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Apply 5x/day for 4 days at first symptom.
Cease if lesions crusted; avoid unnecessary continuation.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Skin

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Major CYP interactions; risk of hepatotoxicity and QT prolongation.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check LFTs baseline and monthly if ongoing.
Avoid with statins, warfarin, or antipsychotics unless monitored.
Document indication, duration, and review date.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Antifungal Therapy

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Chronic methenamine or trimethoprim often continued without review.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Review every 6 months.
Cease if infection-free ≥6 months.
Encourage hydration and toileting regime before restarting prophylaxis.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: eTG Antimicrobial Stewardship | AMS Framework

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Long-term O₂ continued without re-assessment of need or flow rate.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Reassess saturations and need every 3–6 months.
Maintain SpO₂ 88–92 % for COPD; avoid hyperoxia.
Document flow rate, target SpO₂, and review date.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: TSANZ | COPD-X

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Adjunct for Parkinson’s; risk of serotonin toxicity with SSRIs/SNRIs.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Avoid serotonergic combination; monitor BP, mood, hallucinations.
If ineffective after 4 weeks or neuropsychiatric effects occur, taper off.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Neurology

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Selective oestrogen receptor modulator (SERM) for postmenopausal osteoporosis
prevention.
Can cause leg cramps, hot flushes, and increased risk of venous thromboembolism
(VTE).
No proven fracture reduction in non-vertebral sites.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Reserve for women unable to tolerate bisphosphonates or denosumab.
Avoid in residents with history of DVT, PE, or stroke.
Encourage regular mobility and hydration to reduce thrombosis risk.
Cease if prolonged immobility (>2 weeks) or acute illness occurs.
Review bone density and ongoing need every 2 years.

entries.title: Zinc and Vitamin C for Wound Healing

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Extended supplementation after healing → copper deficiency.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Zinc 220 mg daily (max 12 weeks); Vit C 500–1000 mg daily.
Cease once wound closed or after 12 weeks.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: RACGP Wound Care | NHMRC

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Duplication with meals adds unnecessary calories and cost.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use 1–2 serves/day under dietitian direction; review weight monthly.
Stop once BMI > 22 or weight goal met.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: Dietitians Australia | NHMRC

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: High protein formulas for pressure injuries often continued indefinitely.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use for Stage 3–4 ulcers only; review after 4–6 weeks.
Stop if healing achieved or no progress.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: NHMRC Pressure Injury Care | RACGP

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Chronic use in CKD without monitoring → fluid retention.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use only if HCO₃⁻ < 20 mmol/L.
Monitor Na⁺, HCO₃⁻, BP each review; stop if oedema or hypertension worsens.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: eTG Renal | AMH

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Toxicity in renal impairment and drug interactions.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check digoxin level 6–12 monthly (or if symptoms).
Monitor K⁺, Cr, TFTs for amiodarone every 6 months.
Cease if bradycardia or toxicity (signs of nausea, yellow vision).

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Cardiac

entries.title: Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) in Renal Impairment

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Inadequate dose adjustment for renal function significantly increases bleeding risk.
Elderly, low-weight, or renally impaired residents require lower or adjusted dosing.
All DOACs depend on renal clearance to some extent—dabigatran the most,
apixaban the least.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
• Review eGFR every 3–6 months or sooner if clinically unstable.
• Apixaban
• Normal renal function: 5 mg twice daily.
• Reduce to 2.5 mg twice daily if two or more of: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg,
creatinine >133 µmol/L.
• If eGFR 15–30 mL/min: 2.5 mg twice daily (for AF only); avoid <15 mL/min
unless specialist directed.
• Prefer apixaban over other DOACs in moderate renal impairment.
• Rivaroxaban
• If eGFR ≥50 mL/min: standard dose 20 mg once daily (15 mg BD × 3 weeks
for acute DVT/PE).
• If eGFR 15–49 mL/min: reduce to 15 mg once daily for AF; use with caution
for VTE.
• Avoid if eGFR < 15 mL/min.
• Dabigatran
• If eGFR ≥50 mL/min: 110–150 mg twice daily.
• If eGFR 30–50 mL/min: same dose but use lower end in elderly or if on P-
gp/CYP inhibitor.
• Avoid if eGFR < 30 mL/min; dialysis removes 50–60 %.
• Avoid all DOACs if on dialysis or eGFR <15 mL/min unless specialist-approved.
• Warfarin remains preferred for antiphospholipid syndrome or mechanical
valve.
• Watch for drug interactions (antiplatelets, NSAIDs, antifungals, macrolides).
• Re-educate staff to monitor bruising, haematuria, melena, or drop in Hb.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text:
AMH | eTG Anticoagulants | AHA/ASA AF Guidelines | Australian Renal Supportive
Care

entries.title: Anticoagulant Switching and Bridging (Warfarin → DOAC → LMWH)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Incorrect switching between anticoagulants may cause overlap, clotting, or bleeding.
Transition timing depends on drug half-life, INR level, and renal function.
In aged care, changes are often made without clear stop/start documentation or INR
follow-up.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
From Warfarin → DOAC
• Stop warfarin and check INR daily.
• Start DOAC when INR < 2.0 (for apixaban/dabigatran) or <2.5 (for
rivaroxaban).
• Document exact start date and time to prevent overlap.
From DOAC → Warfarin
• Begin warfarin while continuing DOAC for 2–3 days.
• Stop DOAC once INR ≥ 2.0.
• Monitor INR closely for 3–5 days due to variable effect.
From DOAC → LMWH (Heparin / Enoxaparin)
• Stop DOAC and start LMWH 12–24 hours after last dose (longer if renal
impairment).
• For dabigatran, wait 24 hours if eGFR ≥ 50, or 48 hours if eGFR < 50.
From LMWH → DOAC
• Stop LMWH and give first DOAC dose at the next scheduled LMWH dose time.
Perioperative / Bridging Advice
• Stop DOAC 24 hours before minor surgery, 48 hours before major surgery or
neuraxial block.
• Restart once haemostasis achieved (usually 24–48 h post-procedure).
• Bridging with LMWH generally not required for DOACs due to rapid onset.
Clinical Reminders:
• Always document indication, last dose time, and renal function on transfer.
• Reassess indication for anticoagulation after falls, head injury, or recurrent
bleeding.
• For high bleeding risk or renal impairment, liaise with GP or haematologist
before switch.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text:
AMH | eTG Anticoagulants | Thrombosis Australia | AHA/ACC Perioperative
Anticoagulation Guideline

entries.title: Topical Lidocaine or Capsaicin Patches (Local Analgesics)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for neuropathic or localised pain; risk of skin irritation, confusion (if multiple
patches), or dosing errors when left on too long.
Often charted alongside systemic opioids without review of cumulative effect.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use Lidocaine 5% patch up to 12 hours/day (max 3 patches).
Apply only to intact, painful skin; avoid broken skin.
For Capsaicin, educate staff on local burning during first days—improves with use.
Rotate sites; remove old patch before applying new one.
Reassess every 2–4 weeks; cease if no pain reduction.
Document patch timing on MAR to prevent overlap.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Musculoskeletal | RACGP Osteoporosis and Pain Management

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, gout flares, and falls from dehydration.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check Na⁺/K⁺/uric acid 1–2 weeks after changes, then 6-monthly.
Review dose in summer or if dizziness/falls reported.
Avoid in recurrent hyponatraemia.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Headache and postural hypotension leading to falls; tolerance with continuous
dosing.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm angina indication and frequency.
Use lowest effective dose; consider nitrate-free interval for MR products.
Check sitting/standing BP; review if recurrent dizziness.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Can cause bradycardia, heart block, and constipation, especially in older adults or
those already on β-blockers or digoxin.
Often continued long-term for rate control without ECG review or BP monitoring.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check heart rate, BP, and ECG every 6–12 months.
Avoid combining with β-blockers or other negative chronotropes unless specialist-
supervised.
If dizziness, fatigue, or constipation occur, consider switch to amlodipine or
bisoprolol depending on indication.
Taper gradually if used long-term for rate control.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Selective aldosterone antagonist used for heart failure or post-MI LV dysfunction.
Risk of hyperkalaemia and renal decline increases with ACEI/ARB or potassium
supplements.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check U&E and eGFR at baseline, 1 week, 1 month, then every 3 months.
Withhold if K⁺ > 5.0 mmol/L or eGFR < 30 mL/min.
Avoid dual therapy with spironolactone.
If gynaecomastia or confusion on spironolactone, switch to eplerenone at equivalent
dose (25 mg = ~50 mg spironolactone).
Review need at 6 months; deprescribe if stable and euvolaemic.

entries.title: Oral Nutrition Supplements (Ensure , Sustagen , Protein Powders)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Frequently continued after weight stabilisation, increasing calorie load and cost
without benefit.
May suppress appetite or replace balanced meals.
In diabetic residents, excessive carbohydrate formulations can worsen glycaemic
control.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication (weight loss, poor intake, wound healing) and duration.
If used >3 months, review weight trend, dietitian input, and dietary intake records.
Cease or taper if stable weight or intake restored.
Prefer high-protein, low-sugar formulations where diabetes or sarcopenia present.
Ensure administration between meals, not as meal substitute.
Document nutrition goal (e.g., maintain BMI > 22) and reassess every 3 months.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for antibiotic-associated diarrhoea prevention but often continued long-term
without evidence.
Variable strain efficacy; some products contain insufficient colony counts.
Potential infection risk in immunocompromised residents.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use only during and for 1–2 weeks after antibiotic course for prevention of
antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (e.g., Lactobacillus GG or Saccharomyces boulardii).
Avoid chronic daily use without specific indication.
Ensure proper storage (refrigeration if required) and check expiry date.
Cease if diarrhoea resolves or if resident develops infection, immunosuppression, or
severe illness.
Document indication and review at each medication cycle.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Nutrition | RACGP Aged Care Nutrition Guidance

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for heart-failure rate control when β-blockers not tolerated.
Can cause bradycardia, visual brightness (“phosphenes”), or heart block.
Ineffective if AF present.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm sinus rhythm before starting; avoid if resting HR < 70 bpm or BP < 90/50.
Start 2.5–5 mg BD; titrate to HR 50–60 bpm.
Check pulse and BP regularly; review if dizziness or vision symptoms occur.
Cease if AF develops or no symptomatic benefit.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Potent combination for HFrEF but risk of hypotension, hyperkalaemia, and renal
decline.
Interactions with ACEI/ARB; must not be co-administered.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If switching from ACEI, allow 36-hour washout to reduce angioedema risk.
Check U&E/eGFR and BP at baseline, 1 week, and with any dose change.
Titrate gradually (24/26 → 49/51 → 97/103 mg BD).
Avoid if eGFR < 30 mL/min or K⁺ > 5.0 mmol/L.
Monitor for symptomatic hypotension; reduce diuretic dose if needed.
Review at 3–6 months for functional benefit; deprescribe if no clear improvement.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Cardiovascular | Heart Foundation HF Guideline 2022

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Modest benefit for asthma/allergic rhinitis in older adults; neuropsychiatric effects
(agitation, sleep disturbance, low mood) can occur. Often continued without clear
response.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication and document measurable benefit (night symptoms, reliever use).
If no clear improvement after 4–6 weeks, cease.
Avoid in residents with recent mood or sleep changes; review for alternative
(intranasal steroid for rhinitis; ICS/LABA for asthma control).

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for multiple sclerosis (MS) but rarely indicated in aged-care residents.
May cause flu-like reactions, depression, and hepatic enzyme elevation.
Injection-related fatigue and adherence issues common.
Often continued despite minimal functional benefit in late-stage disease.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm ongoing neurology follow-up and current disease-modifying-therapy plan.
If progressive or advanced MS with limited benefit, discuss deprescribing with
neurologist.
Monitor LFTs and mood periodically if continuing.
Ensure cold-chain storage and correct injection rotation to avoid local reactions.
Cease if no clinical or radiological benefit over 6–12 months.

entries.title: Parkinson’s Disease Adjuncts (COMT Inhibitors – Entacapone, Opicapone)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Adjuncts to levodopa that prolong dopamine effect; may cause diarrhoea, vivid
dreams, hypotension, or confusion.
Sometimes continued even when motor benefit uncertain or side-effects outweigh
gains.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication and functional response (e.g., reduced “wearing-off”).
If minimal benefit or troublesome diarrhoea/confusion, consider trial withdrawal
under GP/neurologist supervision.
Monitor for blood pressure drops and hallucinations during review.
Avoid dual COMT inhibitor use; ensure only one agent prescribed.
Maintain levodopa dose timing consistency if adjunct withdrawn.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Neurology | Parkinson’s Disease Management Guidelines

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Residents are at high risk of vaccine-preventable illness, yet boosters are often
overdue or undocumented.
Inconsistent consent and record-keeping can lead to gaps in coverage and reduced
herd protection.
Some residents decline vaccination due to misconceptions or previous mild
reactions.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check immunisation history on AIR (Australian Immunisation Register) each review
cycle.
Ensure the following are up to date:
– Influenza: annual dose (preferably in autumn).
– COVID-19: follow current ATAGI schedule for boosters in ≥65 yrs and high-risk
groups.
– Pneumococcal: single dose of PCV20 or sequential PCV13 + PPSV23 per updated
schedule.
– Shingles (Herpes Zoster): Shingrix 2-dose course, 2–6 months apart, for ≥65 yrs or
immunocompromised.
Document vaccine type, date, and consent clearly in progress notes.
Provide education on side-effects (mild fever, soreness) and manage
symptomatically.
Re-check status annually and coordinate facility vaccination days for efficiency.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for outbreak control (influenza, varicella, shingles), but often continued
unnecessarily after risk period ends.
Renal dose adjustment required; long-term use increases resistance risk.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication and duration (e.g., 10 days for influenza exposure, 7 days for
shingles prophylaxis).
For valaciclovir/acyclovir, reduce dose if eGFR < 50 mL/min.
Cease once outbreak period over or lesions healed.
Avoid prophylactic continuation unless specialist-directed.
Monitor renal function, hydration, and mental status in frail residents.
Document course length, review date, and cessation plan.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Immunisation & Antivirals | ATAGI 2025 Immunisation Schedule

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Narrow therapeutic index; interactions (macrolides, ciprofloxacin), toxicity (nausea,
tremor, arrhythmia, seizures). Clearance reduced in older age and illness.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Avoid initiation where alternatives exist.
If already prescribed, check indication and serum level with any dose/interaction
change; aim lowest effective dose.
Cease if no demonstrable benefit or adverse effects present; switch to inhaled
therapy per COPD/Asthma plan.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Prolonged courses → hyperglycaemia, mood change, infection, osteoporosis.
Adrenal suppression risk if >3 weeks or ≥20 mg/day.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use short bursts for exacerbations (e.g., 25–50 mg daily for 5–7 days, no taper if ≤2
weeks).
If >3 weeks: taper gradually (e.g., reduce by 5 mg each week down to 10 mg, then
2.5 mg steps) while monitoring symptoms/BGL/BP.
Add bone protection review (Ca/Vit D ± bisphosphonate per risk). Document stop
date.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Routine nebulisers increase infection/aspiration risk and deliver higher systemic
doses; technique variability. pMDI + spacer is equally effective for most.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Prefer pMDI + spacer (salbutamol 4–8 puffs q20min in exacerbation) over nebuliser
where possible.
Reserve nebulisers for severe distress or poor pMDI technique; typical doses:
salbutamol 2.5–5 mg neb PRN; ipratropium 250 µg neb in exacerbation.
Enforce infection control: single-patient circuits, clean/dry after each use. Review
ongoing need monthly.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Prolonged corticosteroid therapy (>3 weeks or ≥20 mg/day) suppresses adrenal
function and increases risk of hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis, infection, and mood
changes.
Abrupt withdrawal after long-term use can precipitate adrenal crisis.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
For short courses (≤2 weeks), tapering usually not required.
If used longer, taper gradually over weeks to months depending on duration and
dose:
– Reduce by 5 mg per week down to 10 mg, then by 2.5 mg per week until
cessation.
– Slower taper (1 mg every 2–4 weeks) if long-term or signs of adrenal insufficiency.
Monitor for fatigue, hypotension, nausea, or arthralgia during taper.
Provide bone protection (Calcium/Vit D ± bisphosphonate) and review BGL and BP
regularly.
Ensure clear documentation of indication, duration, and intended stop date.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for metabolic acidosis or urinary alkalinisation but sometimes continued
indefinitely without indication.
Chronic use can cause metabolic alkalosis, sodium overload, and fluid retention,
worsening heart failure or hypertension.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm ongoing indication (e.g., CKD metabolic acidosis, uric acid stone
prevention).
Review serum bicarbonate and electrolytes every 3–6 months.
Avoid in residents with uncontrolled hypertension, oedema, or heart failure unless
closely monitored.
Cease if bicarbonate > 30 mmol/L or no clear clinical benefit.
Encourage hydration and dietary management for acid–base balance.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Frequently continued long-term after an acute hypokalaemia episode without repeat
levels.
High-risk for hyperkalaemia, particularly in CKD or with ACEI/ARB, spironolactone, or
eplerenone.
GI irritation possible with sustained-release tablets.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check serum potassium and renal function at baseline, then after 1 week, monthly
for 3 months, and every 3–6 months if ongoing.
Avoid routine use unless persistent low K⁺ < 3.5 mmol/L with clear cause.
Use oral liquid in swallowing difficulty.
Stop supplement if K⁺ ≥ 5.0 mmol/L or eGFR < 30 mL/min.
Address reversible causes (diuretics, diarrhoea, poor intake) and reinforce dietary
potassium sources instead of chronic tablets.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Nephrology | Kidney Health Australia CKD Management Guidelines

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Long-acting opioid; potency and delayed onset increase risk of sedation, respiratory
depression, and overdose if titrated too quickly.
Often continued despite tolerance or after acute pain has resolved.
Inappropriate for opioid-naïve residents.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Reserve for residents already stabilised on oral opioids ≥ 60 mg oral morphine
equivalent daily (oMEDD).
Start with the lowest patch strength (12–25 µg/hour) and reassess pain, sedation,
and bowel function every 48–72 hours.
Avoid cutting or heat exposure over the patch; dispose via clinical waste (not bin).
Recalculate oMEDD before any change and reduce by 25–50 % during taper.
Review pain management every 3 months; trial wean if pain controlled or function
improved.
Always prescribe a laxative regimen concurrently.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Partial opioid agonist with ceiling effect on respiratory depression; lower misuse
potential.
Transdermal patch (Norspan ) often safer alternative to fentanyl in frail residents,
but may cause nausea, confusion, or skin irritation.
Sublingual formulations (Temgesic ) reserved for acute or breakthrough pain.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
For chronic pain, start with 5 µg/hour patch, titrating slowly at ≥ 7-day intervals.
Do not combine with full opioid agonists unless supervised by pain specialist (risk of
withdrawal or reduced efficacy).
If switching from fentanyl or morphine, calculate equianalgesic dose conservatively
(reduce total by ~50 % for cross-tolerance).
Replace patch every 7 days; ensure removal of old patch before new one.
Monitor for sedation, confusion, constipation, and falls.
Review at least every 3 months for ongoing need or step-down potential.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Analgesia | Palliative Care Guidelines | TGA Safety Update

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Thiamine deficiency may occur with malnutrition, chronic alcohol use, prolonged
diuretic therapy, or post-illness anorexia.
Deficiency can lead to confusion, neuropathy, or Wernicke’s encephalopathy in
vulnerable residents.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Supplement residents with risk factors or poor intake.
Typical oral dose: 100 mg once daily; higher doses (200–300 mg daily) if deficiency
suspected or during refeeding.
If unable to take orally, consider parenteral route (IM/IV) under medical supervision.
Reassess nutrition and hydration; reinforce dietitian referral.
Continue supplementation for at least 2–4 weeks after nutrition improves.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Endocrinology | RACGP Nutritional Deficiency Guidelines

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Commonly used for recurrent UTIs but ineffective if eGFR < 45 mL/min, leading to
poor urine concentration and increased toxicity risk (neuropathy, pulmonary fibrosis,
hepatotoxicity).
Often continued long-term without review or documented indication.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication (prophylaxis vs treatment).
Avoid or cease if eGFR < 45 mL/min or signs of chronic cough, neuropathy, or LFT
derangement.
If prophylaxis required, limit to 3–6 months and review for recurrence.
Encourage hydration and hygiene strategies to reduce recurrence.
Switch to alternative prophylaxis (trimethoprim, methenamine hippurate) if renal
impairment or intolerance.
Monitor renal and liver function every 3–6 months if ongoing.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Effective for simple UTIs but can cause hyperkalaemia, renal impairment, and rash.
Interactions with ACEI/ARB, spironolactone, and methotrexate increase toxicity.
Resistance risk if used long-term for prophylaxis.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Avoid in eGFR < 30 mL/min or with potassium > 5.0 mmol/L.
Check U&E and renal function before starting and during prolonged use.
If prophylaxis used (100 mg nocte), review at 3 months; discontinue if infection-free.
Consider methenamine hippurate as non-antibiotic prophylaxis if suitable.
Document allergy history clearly (rash vs anaphylaxis).

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for oral/vaginal candidiasis but often continued without review or monitoring.
Risk of drug interactions (statins, warfarin, phenytoin, sulfonylureas) via CYP
inhibition.
Accumulation in renal impairment increases toxicity risk (hepatotoxicity, QT
prolongation).

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication and duration (e.g. single 150 mg dose for vaginal; 50–100 mg
daily for oral/esophageal).
Avoid prolonged therapy unless recurrent infection documented.
Adjust dose if eGFR < 50 mL/min (halve maintenance dose).
Monitor LFTs and renal function if >2 weeks therapy.
Check for interactions before adding or ceasing concurrent drugs.
Cease when infection resolved; reassess recurrent thrush for glycaemic control or
denture hygiene issues.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Antimicrobials | RACGP Antimicrobial Stewardship

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Steatorrhoea, bloating, and weight loss from pancreatic insufficiency; doses often
too low or taken incorrectly (not with meals). Crushing/cutting capsules reduces
efficacy.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication (history, stool features, weight).
Start 25,000–40,000 lipase units with main meals; 10,000–25,000 with snacks.
Take with the first mouthful; split across the meal if large/slow eater.
Do not crush; open and sprinkle microspheres only if needed (swallow immediately).
If persistent symptoms at high doses, consider PPI cover and check adherence.
Review weight, stools, gas, and fat-soluble vitamin status at 4–6 weeks.

entries.title: Bowel Preparation Agents (Colonoscopy Prep in Aged Care)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
Suggested Action
fields.text:
Prefer PEG-based solutions (split-dose if possible).
Avoid sodium phosphate; use sodium picosulfate/mag citrate cautiously (ensure
hydration, check eGFR).
Hold or review diuretics, ACEI/ARB, SGLT2 inhibitors on prep day(s) per prescriber
plan.
Use clear-fluid plan with oral rehydration; arrange assisted toileting overnight.
Baseline and post-prep U&E if frail, CKD, or cardiac disease.
Document prep type, volumes taken, adverse events, and falls risk plan.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Widely used for bacterial conjunctivitis, but often continued after symptoms resolve
or prescribed empirically for viral or allergic causes.
Prolonged use can lead to resistance or local irritation.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication (bacterial vs viral/allergic).
Typical course: 1 drop every 2 hours while awake for 2 days, then every 6 hours for 5
days total; ointment at night if required.
Cease after 5–7 days or once symptoms resolve.
Avoid multi-week or prophylactic use.
Ensure separate bottles for each resident; label clearly to prevent cross-
contamination.
Educate staff on sterile drop technique and single-patient supply.

entries.title: Nasal Corticosteroids / Decongestants (e.g. Mometasone, Fluticasone, Otrivin, FESS)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Intranasal steroids are effective for allergic rhinitis but need regular use;
decongestant sprays can cause rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) if used
>5–7 days.
Incorrect technique reduces benefit.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
For allergic rhinitis: use mometasone or fluticasone one spray per nostril daily;
educate on proper use (head slightly forward, aim away from septum).
Avoid decongestant sprays beyond 5–7 days; limit to short-term use for acute
congestion only.
If nasal dryness or epistaxis occurs, check technique and frequency; switch to saline
sprays or add moisturising gel.
Reassess every 3–6 months; deprescribe decongestants if rebound symptoms
persist.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG ENT | Therapeutic Guidelines Allergy & Rhinitis

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Frequent overuse or inappropriate potency selection leads to skin atrophy, bruising,
telangiectasia, and systemic absorption, especially on the face or thin skin.
Under-treatment with weak agents can cause chronic irritation or non-healing
eczema.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Choose the lowest effective potency for site and severity:
• Mild: Hydrocortisone 1% – face, flexures, genital areas.
• Moderate: Methylprednisolone aceponate, Betamethasone valerate 0.02% –
trunk and limbs.
• Potent: Mometasone, Betamethasone dipropionate – thick plaques (psoriasis,
lichen planus).
• Very potent: Clobetasol – short-term only under specialist review.
Apply once or twice daily for up to 7–14 days, then step down or switch to
emollient.
Avoid chronic daily use; taper to intermittent (weekend) therapy for
maintenance.
Educate staff: apply thin layer after bathing, not under occlusion unless
directed.
Reassess every 2–4 weeks; stop if infection or skin thinning occurs.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Fungal infections (intertrigo, tinea, candida) common in aged care. Powders often
overused for moisture control but can cause caking and skin irritation.
Combination antifungal + corticosteroid products increase risk of misuse and
masking infection.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use azole creams (clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole) twice daily until rash
clears plus 7–14 days extra.
Avoid powders for routine prophylaxis; use sparingly for moist folds if no skin break.
Avoid combination steroid/antifungal creams unless short-term (≤7 days) for
inflamed lesions, then switch to antifungal alone.
Promote drying measures: aeration, absorbent dressings, antifungal barrier creams.
Reassess response after 2 weeks; cease once clear.

entries.title: Combination Products Containing Neomycin or Multiple Agents

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Topical antibiotics (e.g., neomycin, bacitracin) and mixed steroid-antibiotic-
antifungal creams increase risk of contact dermatitis, resistance, and masking
infection.
Often used empirically without confirmed bacterial involvement.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Avoid combination products unless infection is confirmed and short-term (<7 days).
Prefer simple emollient + targeted therapy (separate antifungal or steroid as
needed).
Review ongoing use monthly and deprescribe if rash resolved.
If recurrent infection, consider swab for culture and sensitivity.
Document indication, site, and duration in care plan to avoid duplication.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Dermatology | RACGP Skin Management in Aged Care

entries.title: Antiemetic Options Beyond Metoclopramide (Prochlorperazine, Cyclizine, Others)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Choice should match cause (vestibular, migraine, gastroparesis). Many agents have
anticholinergic load, EPS, sedation, or QT prolongation risks. Prochlorperazine
worsens Parkinson’s symptoms.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
• Prochlorperazine (vestibular/migraine): short-term only; watch EPS,
hypotension, sedation; avoid in Parkinson’s and dementia BPSD.
• Cyclizine (motion/vestibular): anticholinergic—use briefly; monitor confusion,
urinary retention, constipation.
• Ondansetron (chemo/post-op/med-induced): useful alternative; monitor QT
prolongation and constipation; avoid with other QT drugs if possible.
• Domperidone (if gastroparesis): consider only if benefits outweigh QT/cardiac
risk; ECG if prolonged use.
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time; avoid duplication with
metoclopramide or other dopamine antagonists. Reassess after 48–72 h;
deprescribe if nausea resolved.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Thyroid, hepatic, pulmonary, ocular, and cardiac conduction adverse effects with
long-term use.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Baseline and 6-monthly: TFT, LFT, ECG; yearly: eye review ± CXR if symptomatic.
Reassess indication if rhythm stable; consider cardiology review for de-escalation.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Narrow therapeutic index; toxicity with renal impairment, dehydration, or
interactions.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check eGFR and digoxin level after dose changes and if symptomatic (nausea,
confusion, bradycardia).
Aim for lowest effective dose; avoid in persistent bradycardia.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: High anticholinergic burden → confusion, constipation, urinary retention, and falls.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Avoid for insomnia or chronic itch; prefer non-sedating alternatives.
Cease if ACB ≥ 2 or cognitive decline present.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Poor inhaler technique reduces benefit; inhaled steroids increase oral thrush risk.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check device technique each review; use spacer for pMDIs.
Rinse mouth after ICS use; record exacerbations and step-down if stable.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Often continued as long-term reflux cover without review or renal dose adjustment.
Dual therapy with a proton-pump inhibitor (PPI + H₂ blocker) provides no additional
benefit and increases risk of confusion, constipation, and drug interactions.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication and review concurrent PPI use — retain the PPI and cease the H₂
blocker unless there is a clear short-term reason (e.g. nocturnal breakthrough reflux
during PPI titration).
Adjust dose for renal function:
• eGFR ≥ 30 mL/min → use standard dose.
• eGFR < 30 mL/min → give 50 % of usual dose or extend interval to every 48 h;
monitor for CNS effects.
For patients on dialysis (HD/HDF/CAPD), treat as eGFR < 30 mL/min.
Trial cessation if asymptomatic and review at follow-up.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Gastroenterology | RACGP Deprescribing Guidelines

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Reliance on PRN-only therapy often leads to impaction, while chronic over-use may
cause diarrhoea, dehydration, or electrolyte imbalance.
Some agents are unsuitable for regular use due to dependence or mucosal irritation.
Choice should be tailored to stool consistency, hydration status, and comorbidities.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Establish a structured regimen combining a maintenance laxative and a PRN “rescue”
option.
Select according to the following principles:
• Safe for regular maintenance:
– Osmotic agents (lactulose, macrogol) – draw water into stool; preferred
long-term.
– Bulk-forming agents (ispaghula, sterculia) – maintain regularity if hydration
adequate.
– Stool softeners (docusate) – gentle aid for hard stools.
• Use intermittently / PRN only:
– Stimulant laxatives (senna, bisacodyl) – effective short-term but risk
abdominal cramps, tolerance, and melanosis coli with chronic use.
– Rectal preparations (glycerol suppositories, enemas) – for rescue or
impaction clearance only.
• Avoid routine use:
– Castor oil or sodium picosulfate for chronic therapy (excessive fluid loss,
electrolyte disturbance).
Monitor bowel chart at least weekly; aim for regular, soft, formed stool.
Encourage fluids, fibre, mobility, and review medications contributing to constipation
(opioids, anticholinergics, calcium supplements).
Reassess need for each product every 3 months and taper when possible.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Gastroenterology | RACGP Aged-Care Constipation Guidelines

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Loperamide may mask infectious diarrhoea (e.g. Clostridioides difficile) and should
not be used when fever, blood, or mucus are present.
Overuse in frail residents can lead to severe constipation, ileus, or abdominal
distension.
Certain antidiarrhoeals are unsuitable for older adults due to anticholinergic or
sedative effects (e.g. diphenoxylate-atropine, codeine phosphate).

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use loperamide only short-term when infection and inflammatory causes are
excluded.
Start with the lowest effective dose (2 mg after each loose stool, up to 8 mg/day);
avoid routine or prophylactic use.
Cease once stool pattern normalises and maintain hydration.
Review concurrent medicines that can cause diarrhoea (metformin, antibiotics,
laxatives, magnesium supplements).
Avoid combination antidiarrhoeals containing opioids or anticholinergics in aged
care.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Gastroenterology | RACGP Aged-Care Guidance

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Recurrent UTI and atrophic symptoms in post-menopausal residents not addressed.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Consider low-dose vaginal oestrogen for urogenital atrophy and recurrent UTI
prevention if no contraindication.
Review symptom relief and UTI frequency at 3 months.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Topical timolol can cause systemic β-blockade leading to bradycardia, hypotension,
and fatigue, particularly when used with oral β-blockers.
Adherence and administration errors are common in residents with poor dexterity or
cognition.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check pulse and blood pressure regularly if timolol is prescribed.
If bradycardic or hypotensive, consider switching to a non-β-blocker agent such as:
• Prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost) – preferred
first-line; once daily, minimal systemic effects.
• Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (dorzolamide, brinzolamide) – useful adjunct or
alternative; monitor for local irritation.
• Alpha-agonists (brimonidine) – may be suitable if prostaglandins not
tolerated, though can cause drowsiness or dry mouth.
Confirm drop technique (punctal occlusion to reduce systemic absorption) and
adherence at each review.
Liaise with optometrist or ophthalmologist before making therapy changes.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH | eTG Ophthalmology | RACGP Aged-Care Medicines Guidance

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Cumulative ACB ≥ 2 increases delirium and falls.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Calculate ACB for all residents on acbcalc.
Prioritise deprescribing of score-2/3 agents (e.g. oxybutynin, TCAs, sedating
antihistamines).

entries.title: Parkinson’s Disease Therapy (Levodopa, Amantadine, MAO-B inhibitors,

fields.text: Dopamine agonists)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Postural hypotension, hallucinations, and confusion may worsen with disease
progression or interacting psychotropics.
Combination therapy increases sedation and fall risk.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Review timing of Levodopa around meals to improve absorption.
Avoid unnecessary dopamine agonists or Amantadine in advanced stages.
Reduce dose if hallucinations, vivid dreams, or confusion occur.
Coordinate changes with neurologist before adjustment.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
High sedation and dizziness risk, especially when combined with opioids or
benzodiazepines.
Often continued when pain no longer neuropathic or stable.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm ongoing neuropathic indication.
Avoid combining with other CNS depressants.
Trial dose reduction if pain stable for >3 months.
Cease gradually to avoid withdrawal.

entries.title: Diabetes – SGLT2 Inhibitors / GLP-1 Agonists (Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin, Semaglutide)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
May cause dehydration, urinary infections, or excessive weight loss in frail residents.
GLP-1 agonists can worsen appetite and GI upset.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check hydration and weight at each review.
Cease or reduce if recurrent infections or excessive weight loss occur.
Use only if clear cardiovascular benefit and renal function adequate (eGFR ≥ 45
mL/min).

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Limited evidence of benefit and high risk of morning sedation or confusion.
Often charted PRN and used nightly.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm indication and frequency of use.
Restrict to short-term trial if non-drug measures fail.
Cease if ineffective after 2 weeks.
Avoid combination with benzodiazepines or opioids.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Often continued indefinitely after stenting or used for primary prevention where
benefit is minimal.
Dual therapy and unprotected use increase GI bleed and anaemia risk, especially
with NSAIDs or anticoagulants.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm current indication and duration.
Cease if used for primary prevention only or beyond guideline period.
If secondary prevention, ensure gastroprotection with PPI and review bleed risk
yearly.
Reassess dual therapy at 12 months post-stent.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Over-treated blood pressure and polypharmacy can cause dizziness, bradycardia,
and falls in frail residents.
Night-time dosing or multiple agents heighten orthostatic hypotension risk.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Aim for relaxed BP targets (< 150/90 mmHg) unless symptomatic.
Check sitting/standing BP and pulse at review.
Simplify to one or two agents; cease duplicates or bedtime doses if postural drop
present.
If HR < 55 bpm on beta-blocker, reduce or cease.

entries.title: Antipsychotics (Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia – BPSD)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
High risk of sedation, cerebrovascular events, and mortality in older adults.
Unclear documentation or absent consent may classify use as chemical restraint.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use only where behaviour poses risk to self or others and non-drug measures fail.
Document diagnosis, indication, and consent clearly in chart and restraint register.
Review every 3 months with goal of dose reduction or cessation.
Avoid Haloperidol in dementia; prefer Quetiapine IR ≤ 75 mg nocte for Parkinson’s
psychosis.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Toxicity risk increases with dehydration, renal impairment, or interacting drugs.
Serum levels often unchecked once mood stabilised.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check renal and liver function and serum level every 6 months.
Cease or reduce if confusion, tremor, or unsteady gait noted.
Avoid combining lithium with diuretics or NSAIDs.
If stable > 12 months, discuss gradual taper with prescriber.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
High total opioid load (> 30 mg oMEDD/day) increases sedation, constipation, and
fall risk.
Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound pain and agitation.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Re-assess pain source and function each review.
Convert to morphine-equivalent dose; reduce by 10–25 % every 1–2 weeks if
appropriate.
Ensure regular laxative and document daily oMEDD total.
Encourage non-opioid options and comfort-based review with GP.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Antibiotics often charted without indication or stop date and continued
unnecessarily.
Prolonged use drives resistance and C. difficile infection.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Record indication, route, and duration for every antibiotic.
Re-evaluate within 48–72 hours for results and switch IV → oral when stable.
Cease or narrow once infection resolved.
Document AMS review and discuss at MAC.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Extended or duplicate use increases extrapyramidal effects, constipation, and QT
prolongation.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Reserve for short-term use only (< 12 weeks).
Avoid Metoclopramide in Parkinson’s or with other QT-prolonging medicines.
Cease if appetite or nausea improved; review ECG if ongoing.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Antimuscarinics raise anticholinergic load causing confusion and constipation.
Tamsulosin can trigger postural hypotension and falls.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Clarify indication — obstruction vs urge incontinence.
For antimuscarinics, review cognition and bowel function every 3 months.
If adverse effects, stop or switch to Mirabegron.
For Tamsulosin, check BP sitting/standing and adjust timing or dose if dizziness
occurs.

entries.title: Vitamins and Supplements (Calcium, Vitamin D, Iron, B12, Folate)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Often continued after correction or duplicated across brands.
Unnecessary use adds cost and risk of constipation or hypercalcaemia.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Verify need with recent pathology before renewal.
Stop or reduce once deficiency resolved.
Combine calcium + vitamin D where possible and avoid multiple iron products.
