Urinary, gastrointestinal, bone/joint and some respiratory infections; Pseudomonas
coverage.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text:
250–750 mg orally every 12 hours or 200–400 mg IV every 12 hours depending on
indication.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Partially metabolised; 40–50% excreted unchanged in urine.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
– eGFR 30–60: Full dose but extend interval if needed (e.g. 12–18 hourly).
– eGFR 15–29: 50–75% of usual dose or extend interval (e.g. 250–500 mg every 18–24
hours).
– eGFR <15: Reduce dose and/or extend interval; for example 250–500 mg every 24
hours.

fields.label: Haemodialysis
fields.text: give 250–500 mg after dialysis.

fields.label: Peritoneal dialysis
fields.text: dose as for eGFR <15.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
Antacids, calcium, iron, zinc (reduced absorption); warfarin (INR changes); QT-
prolonging drugs; steroids (tendon rupture risk); theophylline (increased levels).

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Risk of tendinopathy, QT prolongation, CNS effects and C. difficile. Use cautiously in
older adults, especially with CKD.
🟦 Doxycycline

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text:
Respiratory infections, skin/soft tissue infections, acne, atypical infections, some tick-
borne infections.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 100 mg once or twice daily; often 100 mg twice daily on day 1 then 100 mg daily.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text:
Hepatic and biliary elimination; about 35–60% excreted in faeces and a smaller
proportion in urine.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text: No dose adjustment required at any CKD stage.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: No change; not significantly removed by dialysis.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
Antacids, calcium, iron, zinc (reduced absorption); warfarin (INR changes); retinoids
(intracranial hypertension risk).

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Good choice where renal dosing is difficult. Avoid in severe oesophageal disease
unless taken with water and upright positioning.
🟦 Clarithromycin

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text: Respiratory infections, skin infections, H. pylori eradication.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 250–500 mg twice daily (oral); dose depends on indication.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text:
Hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4 to active metabolite; around 20–40% excreted
unchanged in urine.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
– eGFR 30–60: Standard dosing usually acceptable for short courses.
– eGFR <30: Reduce dose by 50% (for example 250 mg twice daily instead of 500 mg
twice daily).

fields.label: Haemodialysis
fields.text: dose as for eGFR <30; give after dialysis.

fields.label: Peritoneal dialysis
fields.text: same as eGFR <30.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
Potent CYP3A4 inhibitor: increases levels of statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin), some
calcium channel blockers, carbamazepine, some benzodiazepines, warfarin and
others. Risk of QT prolongation when combined with other QT-prolonging drugs.

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Avoid if major interactions present; consider azithromycin or doxycycline instead
where suitable.
🟦 Azithromycin

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text: Respiratory infections, chlamydia, some skin infections, atypical infections.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text:
500 mg on day 1 then 250 mg daily for 4 days, or 500 mg daily for 3 days depending
on indication.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text:
Extensive tissue distribution; largely excreted in bile; about 6–12% excreted
unchanged in urine.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
No dose adjustment required for mild–moderate renal impairment.
In severe CKD (eGFR <10), use with caution but standard doses are generally
acceptable for short courses.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: No specific adjustment; drug not significantly removed by dialysis.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
Less CYP3A4 inhibition than clarithromycin but still some interaction potential; QT
prolongation risk with other QT-prolonging drugs.

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Preferred macrolide in many older CKD patients due to simpler interaction profile.
🟦 Ceftriaxone

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text:
Moderate–severe community-acquired infections including pneumonia, sepsis,
meningitis, UTI, biliary infections.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 1–2 g IV or IM once daily; up to 4 g/day in severe infections.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Dual elimination: biliary and renal; about 30–60% excreted unchanged in urine.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
No adjustment generally required in isolated renal impairment.
When severe renal and hepatic impairment coexist, maximum daily dose is usually
reduced (for example to 2 g/day).

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text:
Not significantly removed by haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis; standard once-
daily dosing usually maintained.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
Calcium-containing solutions (risk of precipitation in IV lines), warfarin (INR change),
nephrotoxic combinations at high doses with other agents.

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Once-daily dosing convenient for RACF residents transferred to hospital in-the-home
or outreach models.
🟦 Piperacillin–Tazobactam

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text:
Severe infections including intra-abdominal, febrile neutropenia, hospital-acquired
pneumonia and sepsis.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 4 g/0.5 g IV every 6–8 hours; extended or continuous infusions used in critical care.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text:
Piperacillin and tazobactam largely renally excreted; both cleared by glomerular
filtration and tubular secretion.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
– eGFR 30–50: 4 g/0.5 g every 8–12 hours.
– eGFR 10–30: 4 g/0.5 g every 12 hours.
– eGFR <10: 2–4 g/0.25–0.5 g every 12 hours depending on severity.

fields.label: Haemodialysis
fields.text:
dose after dialysis; typical 2–3 g/0.25–0.375 g every 12 hours.
Regimens vary and are usually specialist-guided.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
May reduce clearance of methotrexate; interacts with anticoagulants via INR changes;
added nephrotoxicity with other nephrotoxic agents.

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
High sodium load; monitor sodium and fluid balance in heart failure and advanced
CKD.
🟦 Flucloxacillin

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text: Staphylococcal skin and soft tissue infections, osteomyelitis, endocarditis.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 500 mg–1 g every 6 hours orally or IV depending on severity.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Predominantly hepatic metabolism; 10–15% excreted unchanged in urine.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
No formal dose adjustment usually required.
In severe renal impairment (eGFR <10), consider longer dosing interval or lower dose
in very frail patients.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text:
Some removal by haemodialysis; give doses after dialysis if possible, but no routine
major adjustment required.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text: Methotrexate (competition for renal tubular secretion), warfarin (INR changes).

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Cholestatic hepatitis risk, especially with prolonged courses in older adults; monitor
LFTs if therapy is extended.
🟦 Metoclopramide

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text: Nausea, vomiting, gastroparesis, migraine adjunct.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 10 mg up to three times daily.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Partially hepatic; 85% excreted renally (unchanged or conjugated).

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
– eGFR 30–60: 5–10 mg twice daily.
– eGFR <30: 5 mg once or twice daily.
Reduce dose and frequency to avoid extrapyramidal reactions.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: Give reduced doses (5 mg once or twice daily). Not significantly removed by dialysis.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
Antipsychotics (EPS risk), SSRIs/SNRIs (serotonin syndrome), opioids (antagonistic GI
effects).

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
High risk of dystonia and akathisia in older adults. Avoid regular use if possible.
🟦 Domperidone

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text: Nausea, vomiting, gastroparesis.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text:
10 mg three times daily before meals; up to 10–20 mg three to four times daily per
guidelines.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4); renal excretion of metabolites.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
No strict adjustment, but reduce frequency due to prolonged half-life.
For eGFR <30: consider 10 mg once or twice daily.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: Not significantly removed by dialysis; reduced dosing frequency recommended.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
QT-prolonging drugs, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, azoles),
antipsychotics.

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Avoid in frailty or with QT prolongation. Safer than metoclopramide for EPS but
higher QT risk.
🟦 Ondansetron

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text: Nausea, vomiting (post-operative, chemotherapy-related, general nausea).

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 4–8 mg orally or IV every 8–12 hours.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4, CYP2D6 and CYP1A2; metabolites renally excreted.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text: No dose adjustment required.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: No dose change; drug not significantly removed by dialysis.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
Drugs that prolong QT interval, serotonergic agents (serotonin syndrome risk),
apomorphine (contraindicated).

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Can cause constipation and QT prolongation; use cautiously in older adults with
other QT-risk medications.
🟦 Pantoprazole

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text: GORD, peptic ulcer disease, GI protection with NSAIDs or steroids.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 20–40 mg once daily.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Extensive hepatic metabolism; renal excretion of inactive metabolites.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text: No adjustment required.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: No adjustment; not removed by dialysis.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
May reduce absorption of drugs requiring acidic pH (e.g. ketoconazole); reduced
effect of clopidogrel less clinically significant compared to omeprazole.

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Long-term use may increase risk of hypomagnesaemia, fractures and B12 deficiency.
🟦 Omeprazole (or Esomeprazole)

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text: GORD, peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori eradication.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 20 mg once daily; sometimes 20 mg twice daily.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Hepatic metabolism via CYP2C19 and CYP3A4; metabolites renally excreted.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text: No dose adjustment required.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: No adjustment.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
Reduces effect of clopidogrel (CYP2C19 inhibition), increases levels of diazepam and
phenytoin.

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Similar long-term concerns to other PPIs; pantoprazole preferred for fewer
interactions.
🟦 Prednisolone

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text:
Inflammation, COPD exacerbation, asthma, polymyalgia rheumatica, autoimmune
conditions.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 5–60 mg daily depending on condition.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Primarily hepatic metabolism; renal excretion of metabolites.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text: No dose adjustment required.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: No adjustment required.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
NSAIDs (GI bleeding), warfarin (INR fluctuation), SGLT2 inhibitors (infection risk),
diuretics (hypokalaemia).

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Monitor glucose, BP, mood changes, infection risk and fluid retention.
🟦 Dexamethasone

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text:
Inflammation, chemotherapy protocols, severe COVID-19, cerebral oedema, palliative
care.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 0.5–8 mg daily depending on indication.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Hepatic metabolism; metabolites renally excreted.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text: No adjustment required.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: No adjustment.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
Reduced effect of vaccines, increased glucose levels with antidiabetic agents, CYP3A4
inducers/inhibitors.

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
More potent and longer-acting than prednisolone; monitor for mood changes, GI
upset and insomnia.
🟦 Salbutamol (Nebules)

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text: Acute bronchospasm, asthma/COPD exacerbations.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 2.5–5 mg via nebuliser every 4–6 hours or continuous per severity.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Hepatic metabolism; ~75% renally cleared metabolites.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
No specific adjustment, but increased risk of lactic acidosis, tremor and tachycardia in
severe CKD.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: No dose adjustment.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text: Beta-blockers, MAOIs, theophylline, diuretics (hypokalaemia).

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
High doses may cause hypokalaemia and metabolic lactic acidosis; monitor
potassium in frequent use.
🟦 Warfarin

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text:
Prevention and treatment of venous thromboembolism, stroke prevention in atrial
fibrillation, prosthetic heart valves.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text:
Individualised dosing; usually 1–10 mg once daily adjusted to INR (target range
usually 2.0–3.0, or higher for some valves).

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text:
Extensive hepatic metabolism (mainly CYP2C9, also 1A2, 3A4); metabolites excreted
in urine and bile.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
No formal dose adjustment, but sensitivity to warfarin increases as renal function
declines. Start at lower doses in CKD, especially eGFR <30, and titrate carefully to
INR.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: Not dialysed. Dose according to INR, with lower starting doses and close monitoring.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
Many antibiotics (e.g. amoxicillin–clavulanate, macrolides, fluoroquinolones), azoles,
NSAIDs, SSRIs/SNRIs, amiodarone, statins, anticonvulsants, herbal products (e.g. St
John’s wort, ginkgo).

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Renal impairment itself increases bleeding risk; CKD 4–5 and dialysis patients need
particularly close INR and clinical monitoring.
🟦 Dabigatran

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text:
Prevention of stroke and systemic embolism in non-valvular atrial fibrillation;
treatment and secondary prevention of DVT/PE.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text:
150 mg twice daily (or 110 mg twice daily in some higher-bleeding-risk patients,
depending on guideline and age).

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Prodrug converted to dabigatran; about 80% excreted unchanged by the kidneys.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
Because of high renal clearance, accumulation is marked.
– eGFR ≥50: Standard dose (150 mg twice daily or 110 mg twice daily in high
bleeding risk).
– eGFR 30–49: 110 mg twice daily usually preferred.
– eGFR <30: Generally contraindicated or not recommended; avoid in severe CKD.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text:
Not recommended in dialysis; avoid due to unpredictable removal and high bleeding
risk.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
P-gp inhibitors (verapamil, amiodarone, dronedarone, some azoles, some antivirals)
increase levels; P-gp inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John’s wort)
reduce effect; antiplatelets and NSAIDs increase bleeding.

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Among DOACs, dabigatran is the most renally dependent; in older adults with
fluctuating renal function, apixaban is often preferred.
🟦 Edoxaban

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text:
Prevention of stroke and systemic embolism in non-valvular atrial fibrillation;
treatment and prevention of recurrent DVT/PE.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 60 mg once daily.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text:
About 50% excreted unchanged in urine; remainder via biliary and intestinal routes
with minimal CYP metabolism.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
– eGFR 50–80: Standard 60 mg once daily.
– eGFR 15–50: Reduce to 30 mg once daily.
– eGFR <15: Not recommended.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: Not recommended in dialysis patients.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
P-gp inhibitors (e.g. verapamil, quinidine, some macrolides, azoles) may increase
levels; inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) may reduce effect; additive
bleeding with antiplatelets and NSAIDs.

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
Less commonly used than other DOACs in Australia; moderate renal dependency.
🟦 Ibuprofen

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text: Mild–moderate pain, inflammation, fever.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text:
200–400 mg every 6–8 hours as needed; typical maximum 1200–2400 mg/day
depending on indication.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Hepatic metabolism; metabolites excreted by kidneys.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
Use with great caution in eGFR <60; avoid regular use.
– eGFR 30–60: Short courses only at lowest effective dose.
– eGFR <30: Avoid; risk of acute kidney injury and further deterioration in renal
function.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: Generally avoided in dialysis due to residual kidney and cardiovascular risk.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics (triple whammy), other nephrotoxins, warfarin and
other anticoagulants, low-dose aspirin.

fields.label: Other Information
Clinical Use
fields.text: Inflammatory and musculoskeletal pain, arthritis.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 25–50 mg two to three times daily (oral); topical forms also used.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Extensive hepatic metabolism; metabolites excreted mainly in urine and bile.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
Avoid in eGFR <60 for regular systemic use if possible.
– If used at all in eGFR 30–60: lowest dose for the shortest possible time.
– eGFR <30: Avoid systemic diclofenac.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: Avoid systemic use; topical may be considered but systemic absorption still occurs.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
ACE inhibitors/ARBs, diuretics, anticoagulants, other NSAIDs, low-dose aspirin,
methotrexate, lithium.

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
High cardiovascular risk relative to some other NSAIDs; in older CKD patients
systemic diclofenac is usually unnecessary and unsafe.
🟦 Celecoxib

fields.label: Clinical Use
fields.text: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, pain with inflammatory component.

fields.label: Dose in Normal Renal Function
fields.text: 100–200 mg once or twice daily depending on indication.

fields.label: Metabolism
fields.text: Hepatic CYP2C9; metabolites excreted in urine and faeces.

fields.label: Dose in Renal Impairment (eGFR)
fields.text:
– eGFR 45–60: Use lowest effective dose, shortest duration.
– eGFR 30–44: Use with caution; avoid prolonged therapy.
– eGFR <30: Avoid.

fields.label: Dose in RRT
fields.text: Avoid systemic use.

fields.label: Important Drug Interactions
fields.text:
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, anticoagulants, other NSAIDs; CYP2C9 inhibitors may
increase celecoxib levels.

fields.label: Other Information
fields.text:
COX-2 selectivity reduces GI ulcer risk but not renal or cardiovascular risks; same CKD
cautions as non-selective NSAIDs.

Part Focus

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
ARB used for hypertension and kidney protection. May cause hypotension, dizziness,
or hyperkalaemia in frail elderly.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check renal function and potassium.
Cease if BP consistently <110 mmHg or if no clear benefit (e.g. non-diabetic,
normotensive).
Review dual antihypertensive use.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH; RACGP – Managing BP in Elderly

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Similar to irbesartan; used for hypertension, CVD risk, and diabetic nephropathy.
Long half-life.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Cease or consolidate if used with another antihypertensive and BP is low.
Review indication if no albuminuria or end-organ protection required.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines – Hypertension

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
ACE inhibitor commonly continued long-term without regular monitoring. Risk of
hyperkalaemia, cough, hypotension.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Monitor renal function and electrolytes 6-monthly.
Cease or reduce if eGFR <30 or potassium >5.5.
Consider switch to ARB if cough present.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH; Kidney Health Australia

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for nocturnal enuresis or central diabetes insipidus. Risk of hyponatraemia,
especially in elderly.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Ensure indication is still valid.
Monitor sodium levels regularly. Cease if used for night-time urination without
specialist input.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH; TGA Safety Update

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Oral liquid available in 1 mg/mL or as “drops.” Dosing confusion common due to
drops vs mg vs mL labelling.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Chart using mg or mL only — avoid “drops” in orders.
Educate nursing staff on standard syringe usage.
Use smallest effective dose and monitor for sedation.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: Australian Prescriber – Diazepam Oral Liquid Safety Alert

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Frusemide may be added to manage amlodipine-induced leg oedema, but this treats
the side effect rather than solving the problem.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Cease frusemide if only used for peripheral oedema from amlodipine.
Trial dose reduction or switch amlodipine to another antihypertensive.
Monitor weight and fluid balance.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH; NPS MedicineWise

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Frusemide increases urate levels and can worsen or trigger gout flares.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Review if frusemide is essential.
Switch to another antihypertensive or diuretic if possible.
Ensure urate levels and gout symptoms are monitored.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH; RACGP Gout Management Guide

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Some PPIs (e.g. omeprazole) may reduce clopidogrel efficacy. Pantoprazole
preferred. Overuse of high-dose PPI also common.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If gastroprotection needed, ensure use of pantoprazole not omeprazole.
Step down to 20 mg if no ongoing GI bleeding risk.
Review PPI every 6–12 months.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: Therapeutic Guidelines; TGA Safety Statement

entries.title: Statin Use in Secondary vs Primary Prevention

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Statins continued in frail older residents with no CV history, minimal benefit, and
increased risk of muscle pain or falls.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If used for primary prevention, consider cessation.
If secondary prevention, continue if tolerated and indicated.
Request lipid profile before recharting if unsure.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: RACGP Choosing Wisely; AMH

entries.title: Cholecalciferol + Calcium Supplementation in Denosumab Users

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Denosumab requires concurrent vitamin D and calcium to prevent hypocalcaemia.
Often missed or forgotten.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Ensure vitamin D (e.g. cholecalciferol 25 mcg daily) and calcium carbonate 600–1200
mg/day are charted.
Check recent bloods before each dose.
Monitor for constipation if calcium used long term.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: Therapeutic Guidelines – Osteoporosis

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for rheumatoid arthritis or cancer. Fatal errors have occurred from incorrect
daily dosing instead of weekly.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Confirm dose is charted as once WEEKLY, not daily.
Add day of week clearly to chart.
Ensure folic acid is co-prescribed and nursing staff are educated on administration
frequency.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: TGA Safety Alert; AMH

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Narrow therapeutic range. Risk of toxicity increases with dehydration, drug
interactions, or renal decline.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check serum lithium levels every 3 months.
Monitor renal function and thyroid.
Avoid NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors. Cease if specialist review is overdue.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines – Bipolar Disorder

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used only under specialist supervision for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Risk of
agranulocytosis, myocarditis, seizures.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Do not initiate, cease, or adjust in aged care without psychiatrist oversight.
Ensure blood monitoring (FBC, troponin, CRP) is up to date.
Keep emergency protocol accessible for staff.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: TGA; AMH; Clozapine Monitoring Service

entries.title: Warfarin vs DOAC in Frail Residents

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Warfarin requires regular INR monitoring, but often continued in residents with poor
access to pathology or fluctuating diet.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Consider switch to DOAC (e.g. apixaban) if stable renal function and no
contraindication.
Cease anticoagulation if falls risk is extreme and risk outweighs benefit.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: Therapeutic Guidelines – Anticoagulation; AMH

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Used for pain, sleep, or anxiety with limited aged care evidence. Risk of sedation,
confusion, and drug interactions.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Ensure specialist review is in place.
Document indication, consent, and clinical response.
Cease if adverse effects outweigh benefit.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: TGA; Australian Prescriber

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Charted as “drops” or “0.1 mg” without clarity. Nurses may confuse mg vs mL vs
dropper measurements.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Always chart in mg or mL, not “drops.”
Educate staff: 0.1 mg/mL means 1 mL = 0.1 mg.
Use standard syringe, not dropper bottle.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: Australian Prescriber – Clonazepam Liquid Safety

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Crushing MR or enteric-coated tablets (e.g. metformin XR, oxycodone CR,
omeprazole EC) can lead to dose dumping, reduced efficacy, or harm.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check “Don’t Rush to Crush” before crushing any tablet.
Label non-crush meds clearly on chart.
Use liquid or alternate formulation if available.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: SHPA “Don’t Rush to Crush”; AMH

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Residents may be charted for more than one PRN sedative (e.g. oxazepam and
risperidone), with no clear escalation plan or documentation.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Avoid concurrent PRN sedatives.
If both charted, clarify primary use and max daily frequency.
Monitor and document sedation/falls risk.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: Psychotropic Prescribing Guidelines; Aged Care Standards

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Eye drops often stored past expiry or administered improperly (e.g. incorrect spacing
between multiple drops).

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Label bottle with date opened; discard after 28 days unless otherwise stated.
Space drops at least 5 minutes apart when administering >1.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AMH; RACGP Eye Medication Guidelines

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Missed doses frequently lack documented reason (e.g. “refused,” “withheld”),
delaying review or follow-up.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Ensure every missed dose includes a reason.
Flag repeated refusals for pharmacist or GP review.
Track missed doses in audit trail or chart summary.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: ACQSC Medication Management Standard; Facility Policy
Group

fields.label: Examples
fields.text:
1. When to deprescribe Long-term antidepressants, statins, B12, etc.
2. When to add
Gastroprotection with NSAIDs or clopidogrel, laxatives
with opioids
3. Combination cautions Amlodipine + frusemide, PPI + clopidogrel, risperidone +
oxazepam PRN
4. Transition guides
Mirtazapine to duloxetine, amitriptyline to duloxetine
5. High-risk patient
scenarios
Falls after PRNs, crushing issues, confusion around
sedatives

entries.title: When can I stop a resident’s antidepressant?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
If the resident has been stable (no depressive symptoms or episodes) for 12 months
or longer, a tapering trial may be considered.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Taper gradually over 2–4 weeks depending on the agent.
Monitor for withdrawal or mood relapse.
Document rationale and communicate with GP.

entries.title: Should all opioid prescriptions have a laxative?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Yes — opioid-induced constipation is nearly universal without prophylaxis. Regular
laxatives reduce complications and PRN reliance.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Add regular senna/docusate or lactulose at opioid initiation.
If PRN only, review bowel charts weekly and escalate if frequency drops.

entries.title: Does amlodipine cause oedema? Can I give frusemide to fix it?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Yes — amlodipine commonly causes peripheral oedema. But frusemide is not
appropriate unless fluid overload is also present.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Reduce or cease amlodipine. Do not routinely prescribe frusemide for this.
Switch to another antihypertensive class if needed.

entries.title: Do I need gastroprotection if a resident is on clopidogrel?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Yes — if they have a history of GI ulcers/bleeds or are taking additional GI-risk
medications (e.g. SSRIs, NSAIDs, corticosteroids).

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use pantoprazole instead of omeprazole (to avoid CYP2C19 interaction).
Regularly reassess PPI need if bleeding risk changes.

entries.title: Can I give both oxazepam and risperidone PRN for agitation?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Avoid charting multiple PRNs with overlapping sedative effects unless strictly justified
and clearly documented.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Choose one primary PRN.
Document specific scenarios for use (e.g. agitation vs aggression).
Track frequency and effect. Cease or re-chart if used >3×/week.

entries.title: When is gastroprotection (PPI) needed with NSAIDs?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Always consider a PPI if the resident is taking NSAIDs and has:
•
Age ≥65
•
History of GI bleed or ulcer
•
Concurrent corticosteroid or anticoagulant use

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Prescribe pantoprazole 20 mg daily while NSAID is charted.
Review every 3–6 months and cease if NSAID is stopped.

entries.title: What’s the difference between regular vs PRN paracetamol for chronic pain?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Regular dosing may be useful short-term for established arthritis or known chronic
pain.
PRN allows flexibility and reduces unnecessary exposure.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use regular dosing short-term (e.g. 1–2 weeks) after flare or fracture.
Cease or convert to PRN once pain is under control.

entries.title: Is melatonin safer than benzodiazepines for sleep?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Yes — melatonin 2 mg MR is a safer alternative for short-term insomnia or sleep
pattern disruption in dementia.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Cease benzodiazepine and trial melatonin for 2–4 weeks.
Monitor for changes in sleep pattern and adjust care plan accordingly.

entries.title: Can antidepressants prescribed for chronic pain?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Yes — agents like duloxetine or amitriptyline have evidence in neuropathic or
fibromyalgia-type pain, especially when mood overlap exists.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Start low (e.g. duloxetine 30 mg daily).
Review pain chart and mood symptoms after 2–4 weeks.
Avoid tricyclics in frail elderly due to anticholinergic burden.

entries.title: What should I do if an MR tablet is crushed accidentally?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Crushing a modified-release (MR) tablet can result in dose dumping or treatment
failure.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Notify GP and pharmacist immediately.
Monitor for adverse effects or signs of overdose.
Re-chart formulation (e.g. liquid or IR alternative) if swallowing issues are ongoing.

entries.title: How often should I monitor renal function for high-risk meds?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
For medications like digoxin, metformin, lithium, or SGLT2 inhibitors, eGFR should be
checked every 3–6 months in residents aged ≥75 or with fluctuating fluid status.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Set a review reminder in clinical software.
Cease or adjust doses based on trend, not just one-off values.
Collaborate with GP if renal decline noted.

entries.title: When is it appropriate to trial ceasing a statin?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
If used for primary prevention in frail, elderly residents with limited life expectancy
and no history of CV disease — benefit may no longer outweigh risk.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Discuss with GP. Cease if fatigue, myalgia, or no clear indication.
Keep secondary prevention statins if well tolerated and recent CV event.

entries.title: What do I do if a medication is repeatedly refused?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Frequent refusals (>3×/week) without clinical follow-up risk under-treatment or
mismanagement.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Document refusal reason.
Notify GP and pharmacist for deprescribing or formulation change (e.g. ODT or
liquid).
Review whether the medication is still needed.

entries.title: How should I chart PRN medications with maximum frequency?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
All PRNs must include a maximum frequency (e.g. “every 6 hours, up to 3
times/day”).

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Avoid vague charting like “PRN” without dose intervals.
Include “monitor effect” or “document reason for use” in chart or MAR.

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Not all tablets are safe to crush. MR, EC, or cytotoxic meds may be harmful or
ineffective when altered.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use Don’t Rush to Crush guide or confirm with pharmacist.
Switch to liquid, ODT, or alternative if crushing is unsafe.
Always label “Do Not Crush” meds clearly on chart.

entries.title: Is anxiety the same as agitation?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
No.
Anxiety = internal worry, fear, nervousness.
Agitation = physical restlessness, pacing, irritability, motor tension.
A resident may be agitated without feeling anxious (e.g., pain, constipation, unmet
needs).

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Link anxiety and agitation to the correct diagnosis (dementia, delirium, pain, GAD).
Do not use agitation as a diagnosis.

entries.title: Is anxiety in dementia the same as GAD?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
No.
In dementia, anxiety behaviours usually represent BPSD symptoms or unmet needs,
not psychiatric GAD.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Document:
Diagnosis: Dementia

fields.label: Indication
fields.text:
BPSD – anxiety/restlessness
Avoid SSRIs/buspirone unless a true mood/anxiety disorder is confirmed.

entries.title: How do I tell the difference between anxiety and panic disorder?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Panic disorder involves sudden, intense episodes of fear with physical symptoms
(palpitations, sweating, choking, chest tightness).
Anxiety is gradual, persistent, and less intense.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Document panic attacks explicitly.
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines to “prevent” panic.

entries.title: What is the difference between psychosis and hallucinations?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Psychosis is a diagnosis category (schizophrenia, schizoaffective, bipolar with
psychosis, late-onset psychosis).
Hallucinations are a symptom/indication.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Document:
Diagnosis: Psychosis or dementia or delirium

fields.label: Indication
fields.text:
Hallucinations/delusions
Never write hallucinations as diagnosis.

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Psychosis is not the final diagnosis — it is a clinical syndrome.
The underlying diagnosis must be specified:
– schizophrenia
– schizoaffective disorder
– bipolar disorder with psychotic features
– late-onset psychosis
– delirium
– dementia (Lewy body, Parkinson’s)

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text: Avoid using “psychosis” as the sole diagnosis on a psychotropic order.

entries.title: What is the difference between schizophrenia and paraphrenia?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Schizophrenia = early adulthood onset, cognitive decline, negative symptoms.
Paraphrenia = late-onset psychosis with preserved personality, often delusions with
fewer negative symptoms.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use modern term: late-onset psychosis.
Indication = hallucinations/delusions.

entries.title: What is the difference between psychosis and paranoia?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Paranoia = a type of delusion (persecutory belief).
Psychosis = a loss of reality, which may include paranoia but also hallucinations,
disorganised thinking, etc.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If paranoia only → document “delusional thinking.”
If paranoia + hallucinations → document “psychotic symptoms.”

entries.title: Is agitation a diagnosis or an indication?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Agitation = indication, not a diagnosis.
It is a behavioural state triggered by dementia, delirium, pain, anxiety, environment.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Document underlying cause.
If dementia: BPSD – agitation.
If delirium: agitation secondary to delirium.

entries.title: Is aggression a diagnosis or an indication?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text: Aggression = indication, not a diagnosis.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Dementia → BPSD – aggression
Delirium → aggression related to delirium
Pain → behavioural response to pain

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
No.
BPSD is an indication describing behavioural symptoms caused by dementia.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Always specify:
Diagnosis: Dementia

fields.label: Indication
fields.text: BPSD – [specific behaviour]

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
No — paranoia is a symptom (a type of delusion).
It occurs in dementia, psychosis, delirium, or severe depression.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Document the underlying diagnosis and treat causes (infection, dehydration, sensory
loss, delirium).

entries.title: Is "calling out", "wandering", "exit-seeking", "restlessness" a diagnosis or indication?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text: They are all behavioural symptoms, not diagnoses.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Identify cause: dementia, pain, fear, delirium, boredom, loneliness.
Document behaviour under BPSD when linked to dementia.

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
No — it is a legal classification when a medication is used primarily to control
behaviour.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
To avoid restraint classification:
– Always document the actual clinical diagnosis
– Always specify the exact indication (BPSD – agitation, delusions, hallucinations)

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text: No — it is a restrictive practice involving physical/environmental limitation.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text: Document rationale, consent, and alternatives.

entries.title: How do I tell the difference between anxiety and agitation?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Anxiety is an internal emotional state (fear, worry, nervousness).
Agitation is a physical motor state (pacing, fidgeting, restlessness, irritability).

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If the resident can express fear or worry → anxiety.
If restlessness occurs without clear emotional distress → agitation.
Document the correct indication and link to a diagnosis (dementia, delirium, pain,
GAD).

entries.title: How do I distinguish depression from apathy?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Depression involves sadness, hopelessness, guilt, tearfulness, low mood.
Apathy is reduced motivation and initiative without emotional sadness — common
in dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and ageing.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If mood is normal but motivation is low → apathy (no antidepressant needed).
If mood is persistently low → consider depression diagnosis.
Record symptoms carefully to avoid inappropriate SSRI use.

entries.title: What is the difference between delirium and dementia?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and almost always caused by medical illness (infection,
dehydration, medication).
Dementia is chronic, progressive, and stable day-to-day.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If sudden deterioration → treat as delirium.
If baseline cognitive decline → dementia.
Do not label delirium behaviours as BPSD.

entries.title: How do I tell sundowning from agitation?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Sundowning is late-afternoon confusion, anxiety, or restlessness related to
dementia’s circadian disruption.
Agitation can occur at any time and may have other triggers (pain, environment,
fear).

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If symptoms happen consistently in the late afternoon or evening → sundowning.
Document as:

fields.label: Indication
fields.text: BPSD – late-day restlessness (sundowning)

entries.title: What is the difference between hallucinations and illusions?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Hallucinations = seeing/hearing something that is not there.
Illusions = misinterpreting something that is actually there (e.g., coat on chair
becomes “a person”).

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Illusions often indicate sensory impairment or Lewy body dementia.
Hallucinations require assessment for dementia, delirium, psychosis, or medications.

entries.title: How do I know if behaviour is due to pain?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Pain often presents as behaviour in residents with dementia or communication
limitations:
– grimacing
– refusing care
– guarding
– calling out
– restlessness
– resisting movement
– aggression

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Trial analgesia before psychotropics.
Document:
“Behaviour likely pain-related — responded to analgesia.”

entries.title: How do I tell if agitation is from constipation or unmet needs?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Constipation-driven agitation is common and presents with:
– restlessness
– irritability
– pacing
– inability to sit
– abdominal discomfort
– reduced appetite
Unmet needs (toileting, cold, hunger, thirst, loneliness) can look identical.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Check bowels, hydration, toileting, pain, and comfort before considering
psychotropics.
Document findings and interventions.

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Typically no.
Calling out is usually due to distress, loneliness, pain, anxiety, or inability to
communicate needs.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Record the underlying cause.
Avoid charting psychotropics for calling out alone.

entries.title: How do I tell the difference between panic episodes and agitation?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Panic episodes involve:
– sudden fear
– trembling
– palpitations
– shortness of breath
– sense of doom
Agitation:
– pacing
– restlessness
– irritability
– motor tension
– confusion

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If symptoms are sudden and fear-driven → panic.
If confused/restless → agitation likely due to dementia or delirium.

entries.title: What is the difference between paranoia and psychosis?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Paranoia is a type of delusion (feeling threatened or persecuted).
Psychosis is a syndrome involving paranoia, hallucinations, or disorganised thinking.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
If paranoia occurs in dementia → BPSD – delusions.
If paranoia is primary → consider psychotic disorder.

entries.title: How do I distinguish depression from grief?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Grief involves sadness but preserves self-esteem, and symptoms fluctuate.
Depression involves persistent low mood, guilt, hopelessness, and functional decline.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Document grief as a normal emotional process unless symptoms become persistent
or impairing.

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
No — it is a behaviour.
The diagnosis maybe dementia.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Record:
“BPSD – wandering/exit seeking”
if related to dementia.

entries.title: How do I distinguish insomnia from agitation or psychosis?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Insomnia = cannot fall/stay asleep.
Agitation = restlessness, irritability.
Psychosis = hallucinations/delusions interfering with sleep.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text: Investigate cause of sleeplessness before medicating.

entries.title: Is emotional distress the same as a mental illness?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
No.
Distress may arise from loneliness, pain, fear, unmet needs, grief, or environment.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text: Treat causes before considering psychiatric diagnosis.

entries.title: How do I tell if behaviours are due to delirium instead of dementia?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Delirium = sudden onset, fluctuating consciousness, inattention.
Dementia = slow, stable decline.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text: If sudden change → delirium until proven otherwise.

entries.title: Is refusing care a psychiatric symptom?

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Not necessarily.
Refusal often reflects fear, pain, trauma history, cultural differences, or inability to
understand instructions.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text: Document cause and use behavioural strategies before psychotropics.

entries.title: “If a doctor writes ‘palliative care’ as the reason for midazolam, quetiapine, or

fields.text: morphine, is it chemical restraint?”

fields.label: Clarification
fields.text:
Not automatically — it depends on intent.
If the purpose is symptom relief (pain, dyspnoea, terminal agitation), it is not
restraint.
If the purpose is behaviour control (agitation, wandering, calling out), it is restraint.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Document the specific palliative symptom being treated.
Avoid writing “behavioural issues” or “agitation” without a clinical explanation.

entries.title: When is a palliative medication not considered chemical restraint?

fields.text:
A palliative medication is not chemical restraint when it is prescribed to relieve a
clinical palliative symptom. These symptoms arise from the dying process or
advanced disease, not from behaviour.
Common palliative symptoms include:
• Pain
• Dyspnoea
• Terminal secretions
• Nausea
• Vomiting
• Anxiety related to end-of-life distress
• Terminal agitation due to the physiological dying process
• Respiratory discomfort
• Severe nausea
• Seizures

fields.label: Examples
fields.text:
Morphine prescribed for dyspnoea in end-stage heart failure is not chemical
restraint.
Midazolam used for terminal agitation is not chemical restraint.
Haloperidol used for palliative delirium or end-of-life nausea is not chemical
restraint.
Hyoscine used for terminal secretions is not chemical restraint.
These uses are exempt because the intent is symptom relief, not behaviour control.

entries.title: When can palliative medications still be classified as chemical restraint?

fields.text:
Palliative medications are chemical restraint if they are used primarily to control
behaviour, even if the resident is labelled as “palliative” or “comfort care.”

fields.label: Examples
fields.text:
• Quetiapine used to stop wandering
• Lorazepam used to stop calling out
• Antipsychotics used to sedate a resident for staff convenience
• Sedation used because the resident is “difficult to manage”
The assessment question is:
Is the medication being used to relieve a documented palliative symptom, or is it
being used to make the person easier to manage?
If the purpose is behaviour control without a clinical symptom, it is classified as
chemical restraint.

entries.title: How should palliative medications be documented to avoid chemical restraint

fields.text:
classification?
Accurate documentation is essential.
1. The underlying diagnosis
Examples include:
– End-stage dementia
– Metastatic cancer
– End-stage heart failure
– Palliative phase of Parkinson’s disease
– Advanced frailty
2. The specific symptom being treated
Examples include:
– Pain
– Dyspnoea
– Terminal agitation
– Nausea or vomiting
– Secretions
– Seizures
– Anxiety associated with end-of-life discomfort
3. The purpose of the medication
A clear purpose statement should be documented, such as:
“The medication is prescribed to relieve distressing symptoms related to the
dying process.”
If a symptom is documented, the use is not chemical restraint.
If the behaviour alone is documented (such as agitation, wandering, calling out), it
may be classified as chemical restraint.

entries.title: Which medications are commonly used in palliative care, and what are their

fields.text:
indications?
Opioids
Morphine – pain, dyspnoea
Hydromorphone – pain
Oxycodone – pain
Fentanyl – chronic severe pain
Methadone – pain, opioid rotation
Benzodiazepines
Midazolam – terminal agitation, seizures, dyspnoea
Diazepam – seizures, muscle spasm
Antipsychotics
Haloperidol – palliative delirium, nausea, agitation
Risperidone – mild delirium
Olanzapine – nausea, delirium, agitation
Anticholinergics
Hyoscine hydrobromide – terminal secretions
Glycopyrrolate – secretions, spasms
Anti-emetics
Metoclopramide – nausea
Ondansetron – nausea
Haloperidol – nausea and delirium
Steroids
Dexamethasone – appetite stimulation, nausea, inflammation-related pain
Anticonvulsants
Levetiracetam – seizures
Valproate – seizures
Other agents
Paracetamol – pain, fever
NSAIDs – pain
Scopolamine – secretions, nausea

General Principles
• Type 1 diabetes requires lifelong insulin because the pancreas produces no insulin.
• The correct model is basal–bolus therapy (long-acting + rapid-acting insulin).
• Sliding scale must not be used alone in Type 1.
• Carbohydrate counting and dose adjustment are essential.
• Insulin must never be stopped — even when the patient is not eating (give basal
insulin).
Basal (Long-Acting) Insulin in Type 1
Used to provide background insulin 24 hours a day.

fields.label: Examples
fields.text: Glargine (Lantus), Detemir (Levemir), Degludec (Tresiba), NPH.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.text:
Maintain fasting levels, suppress hepatic glucose production.
Key points:
• Given once daily (some twice, depending on insulin).
• Do NOT adjust based on meals.
• Adjust based on fasting glucose trend over 2–3 days.
Bolus (Short-Acting / Rapid-Acting) Insulin in Type 1

fields.label: Examples
fields.text: Aspart (Novorapid), Lispro (Humalog), Glulisine (Apidra), Regular insulin.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.text:
Cover carbohydrate intake and correct high blood glucose.
Principles:
• Dose before meals.
• Use insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio (e.g. 1 unit per 10–15 g CHO).
• Use correction factor (e.g. 1 unit reduces BGL by 2–3 mmol/L).
Sliding Scale in Type 1
Sliding scale must not be used as the only insulin regimen in type 1.
If sliding scale is used, it must be:
• Temporary
• Added on top of a scheduled basal–bolus regimen
Never use sliding scale alone in Type 1 — risk of ketoacidosis.

entries.title: Preventing Hypoglycaemia and Hyperglycaemia in Type 1 Diabetes (with CGM Integration)

fields.text:
Type 1 diabetes requires uninterrupted insulin therapy. Prevention of hypoglycaemia
and hyperglycaemia relies on consistent basal insulin, accurate meal dosing,
recognition of patterns, and close monitoring, particularly during illness. Continuous
Glucose Monitoring (CGM) enhances safety by providing real-time glucose trends.

Hypoglycaemia occurs when insulin exceeds carbohydrate intake or metabolic
demand. Prevention requires attention to dosing, intake variability, and activity levels.
1. Basal insulin must never be omitted
Basal insulin prevents ketosis and stabilises overnight glucose.
Omitting it increases the risk of rebound hyperglycaemia and later hypo due to
overcorrection.
2. Match rapid-acting insulin to food intake
Reduce bolus insulin if the resident eats less than usual.
Withhold bolus insulin if no carbohydrate is eaten, while always continuing basal
insulin.
3. Adjust insulin for physical activity
Exercise, wandering, and restlessness increase insulin sensitivity.
Provide additional carbohydrates or reduce pre-activity bolus doses.
4. Review doses after any hypoglycaemic event
Repeated lows at similar times indicate excessive dosing.
• Overnight hypoglycaemia → basal dose too high
• Post-meal hypoglycaemia → bolus dose too high
5. Avoid insulin stacking
Rapid-acting insulin should not be re-dosed within 2–3 hours unless directed for
correction.
6. Consider renal impairment, frailty, and weight loss
Reduced muscle mass and declining renal function increase insulin sensitivity.
7. Use CGM to detect falling trends early
CGM arrows showing rapid decline allow intervention before hypoglycaemia
develops.
Overnight lows are reliably detected by CGM, preventing unrecognised
hypoglycaemia.

Hyperglycaemia usually results from insulin deficiency, missed boluses, illness, or
steroid use. Preventing high glucose is essential to reduce the risk of DKA.
1. Ensure basal insulin is always administered
Basal insulin omission is one of the most common causes of hyperglycaemia and
ketosis.
2. Give bolus insulin before meals
Delayed or missed bolus insulin leads to significant post-meal spikes.
Pre-meal dosing (10–15 minutes before eating) yields better glucose control.
3. Adjust doses based on glucose trends
• High fasting glucose → increase basal
• High post-meal readings → increase bolus
Dose changes should follow consistent patterns, not single readings.
4. Apply sick-day rules
During illness, glucose rises due to counter-regulatory hormones.
Insulin must not be reduced; doses often need to be increased.
Ketone testing is required for persistent hyperglycaemia.
5. Review insulin potency and injection site health
Expired or heat-damaged insulin can cause poor control.
Lipohypertrophy causes erratic absorption; rotate injection sites.
6. Avoid sliding scale as sole therapy
Sliding scale reacts to elevated BGL without preventing ongoing highs.
It must be used only temporarily and only alongside basal insulin.
7. Use CGM to detect rising glucose early
CGM allows early identification of post-meal spikes and persistent highs.
Trend arrows help determine whether levels are stable or increasing rapidly.

entries.title: How Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) Enhances Glycaemic Safety

fields.text:
CGM provides near-continuous glucose readings and directional trends, improving
the detection and prevention of both hypo- and hyperglycaemia.
1. Trend arrows allow early intervention
• Falling trend → reduce mealtime insulin or give carbohydrate
• Rising trend → adjust bolus insulin or monitor for illness effects
2. Alerts prevent severe hypoglycaemia
CGM alarms notify staff before BGL becomes dangerously low, particularly overnight.
3. Improved post-meal management
CGM reveals whether bolus doses are adequate based on the post-prandial curve.
4. Enhanced safety during illness
Glucose rises rapidly during infection or dehydration.
CGM enables frequent monitoring without excessive finger-pricks.
5. Pattern recognition for dose adjustments
• Recurrent highs → adjust basal or bolus
• Recurrent lows → reduce insulin doses
CGM provides a clearer pattern over days rather than isolated values.
6. Supports residents with cognitive impairment
CGM reduces missed checks and identifies nocturnal or unrecognised
hypoglycaemia.
7. Confirms accuracy of treatment decisions
Use finger-prick testing only when symptoms do not match CGM readings or
readings are extreme.

• CGM may lag during rapid glucose changes.
• Compression artefacts can cause false low readings at night.
• Sensors require correct placement and regular replacement.
• Finger-prick confirmation is required if readings appear inconsistent.
When to escalate care
• Recurrent hypos despite reductions in insulin
• Persistent hyperglycaemia (>15 mmol/L)
• Presence of ketones
• Vomiting with high glucose
• Illness not responding to usual adjustments
• Unclear insulin needs or mismatched trends

Part 1 – Audit Templates
Includes structured templates for falls audits, psychotropic audits, opioid utilisation
review, swallowing risk assessments, antibiotic stewardship checks, and medication
chart quality audits.
Part 2 – MAC Meeting Preparation and Reporting
Provides frameworks for preparing monthly MAC summaries, trend analysis, incident
review alignment, and presentation formatting for DON and GP attendees.
Part 3 – Policy Review Templates
Contains templates for reviewing facility policies, including medication management,
restrictive practices, opioid safety, psychotropic governance, and high-risk
medication procedures.
Part 4 – Staff Training Frameworks
Outlines structured education modules for RN and PCA upskilling, including
medication safety, PRN documentation standards, swallowing safety, pain
assessment, and restrictive practice compliance.
Part 5 – SMART Goal Templates for Pharmacist Governance
Provides SMART goal examples for quality improvement initiatives, medication
governance priorities, deprescribing outcomes, and audit follow-through tracking.

difficulties.

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text:
Falls remain one of the highest-risk clinical indicators in aged care.
Audit data often shows mismatched reporting between iCare and physiotherapy
logs, as well as medication-linked falls involving sedatives, opioids, or psychotropics.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Use the standard “Falls Audit Data” Excel sheet with these columns only:
Resident name | Opioid | Benzodiazepine | Co-sedatives | Psychotropic | Blood
thinner | ACB | oMEDD (mg/day) | Avg BP | Avg BGL | Comments
Ensure each field is completed accurately (Y/N or numerical).
Highlight any resident with ACB ≥ 2 or oMEDD ≥ 30 mg/day for GP review.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: ACQSC QI Program | RACGP Falls & Medication Risk | Eloquence v3

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: Lack of visual summary makes trend comparison difficult.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Create the following charts directly from the Data sheet:
1. Clustered Column: iCare vs Physio Falls totals.
2. Stacked Column: Exposure to fall-risk medication classes (Opioid, Benzo, Co-
sedatives, Psychotropic, Blood thinner).
3. Clustered Column: oMEDD risk bands (0 / 1–29 / ≥ 30 mg).
4. Clustered Column: ACB burden bands (0–1 / 2–3 / ≥ 4).
Include counts and percentage labels. Use consistent colours (navy/teal/grey).

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: Facility Audit Framework | PPA QUM Program

entries.title: Falls Audit – Narrative Example (to include in MAC minutes)

fields.label: Issue to Consider
fields.text: High sedative load and incomplete documentation between iCare and physio logs.

fields.label: Suggested Action
fields.text:
Summarise audit in MAC report:
“The quarterly falls audit reviewed 20 residents.
35 % had moderate–high opioid burden (≥ 30 mg oMEDD/day).
10 % had ACB ≥ 2.
Documentation mismatches identified between iCare and Physio logs; reconciliation
completed.”
Add 3–5 bullet-point recommendations:
• Rationalise sedative/psychotropic therapy.
• Ensure same-day reconciliation of fall incidents.
• Educate staff on linking PRN use to post-fall reviews.
• Reinforce BGL/BP monitoring after any fall.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: ACQSC Quality Indicator Program | MAC Governance Manual

Inconsistent reporting of QI metrics and limited linkage between audit findings and
clinical action plans.
Use the following sub-sections each month in MAC meeting minutes:
1. Falls
Summarise audit results (from Falls sheet).
Include total residents with ≥ 1 fall, % linked to medications, and reconciliation
count.
2. Psychotropics
Compare facility antipsychotic use to national QI benchmarks.
Display a clustered column chart with:
• Antipsychotic use (%)
• Antipsychotic + psychosis diagnosis (%)
• National averages.
3. Polypharmacy
Chart quarterly polypharmacy rates (≥ 9 meds) vs national average.
Comment on deprescribing actions from CMRs.
4. Medication Review Activity & Impact
List number of CMRs, follow-ups, dose reductions, and duplications resolved.
Link outcomes to improved QI results.
5. Recommendations / Next Steps
• Schedule GP review for residents with high sedative load.
• Reconcile all falls within 24 h.
• Deliver staff education on restraint consent and PRN documentation.

fields.label: Reference
fields.text: AIHW QI Benchmark Data

“During this period, 39 CMRs were completed.
Facility antipsychotic use (any) was 11.3 % vs national 17.8 %.
Polypharmacy (≥ 9 meds) 33 % vs national 35.2 %.
Targeted deprescribing and improved reconciliation reduced sedative load and fall
recurrence.”

Use two charts for presentation:
1. Quality Indicators – Antipsychotic Use (Quarterly Comparison)
2. Quality Indicators – Polypharmacy (Quarterly Trend)
Keep same y-axis (0–50 %) for readability.

Use this when verbally briefing MAC, or RN team:
“This quarter I completed 14 resident reviews.
– Psychotropic use dropped from 18 % → 14 %, below national average (22 %).
– Three falls occurred within 2 hours of PRN sedative use, improved from last
quarter’s five.
– Two antibiotics lacked charted duration; follow-up done with GPs.
– Education provided on PRN charting and medication crushing safety.
Key priorities next quarter include opioid taper review and monitoring new
admissions for psychotropic prescribing.

entries.title: SMART Goal Framework for Aged-Care Pharmacists

fields.text:
1. Monthly Clinical Focus Example
Each month, identify one focused area of practice improvement. For instance, a
pharmacist might aim to review all residents prescribed two or more PRN
psychotropics to ensure that documentation and rationale are appropriate.
The measurable target could be to complete at least twelve such reviews within the
month. The goal remains achievable by concentrating on one or two facility wings
each fortnight, while staying relevant to psychotropic safety and restraint
minimisation priorities.
All findings should be finalised by the end of the month and presented at the next
MAC meeting.
2. Deprescribing Project Example
A second SMART goal might address medication simplification. For example, plan to
cease unnecessary long-term vitamin supplementation.
Success can be measured by reviewing at least six residents and recording clear
recommendations for each. The task is achievable during regular medication chart
and care-plan reviews, and it remains relevant to the QUM framework and broader
deprescribing initiatives.
The project should be completed by the end of the audit quarter and included in the
Quality-Improvement report.
3. Ongoing Goal Tracker
Keep a concise record of focus areas month by month. Note the target domain, your
intended outcome, and the completion status.
For example:
• May: focus on psychotropics—reduce frequent PRN use; outcome: three re-
charted, two ceased.
• June: focus on supplements—rationalise vitamins; outcome: in progress,
consent pending for two residents.
This running log helps demonstrate continuous improvement and provides evidence
of pharmacist engagement across successive MAC cycles.

Each entry will include:
1. Resident Summary Table
2. Issue to Consider (max 1–2 short lines)
3. Suggested Action (clear, non-repetitive)
4. Clinical Reasoning (brief paragraph explaining rationale and wording choices)

entries.title: Clonazepam Oral Liquid – Drops vs mg vs mL

fields.label: Common Error
fields.text:
Dose charted as “10 drops” or “0.1 mg” without specifying volume. Nurses may
confuse drops, mL, and mg, especially with different bottle types (e.g. 0.1 mg/mL).

fields.label: Real Risk
fields.text:
Significant sedation or underdosing in frail residents. No standardisation across
brands.

fields.label: Suggested Fix
fields.text:
Always chart as mg or mL only (e.g. “0.1 mL = 0.01 mg”)
Never chart “drops”
Train staff to use oral syringe — not dropper bottle
Add admin tip to chart: “Use syringe. Do not use drops.”

fields.label: Reference
fields.text:
Australian Prescriber: Clonazepam oral liquid – confusion between drops, milligrams
and millilitres.

entries.title: Paracetamol Oral Liquid – Dose in mg vs volume

fields.label: Common Error
fields.text:
Paracetamol liquid charted as “500 mg” but no volume given. Staff unsure if 5 mL or
10 mL is correct.

fields.label: Real Risk
fields.text: Underdosing or inconsistent dosing, especially in PRN use for pain or fever.

fields.label: Suggested Fix
fields.text:
Write as: “500 mg = 5 mL” clearly in MAR
Check that label strength matches chart
Reinforce: “Check label strength before drawing dose”

fields.label: Common Error
fields.text: Warfarin dose charted as “1 tab” without strength (e.g. 1 mg? 2 mg? 5 mg?).

fields.label: Real Risk
fields.text:
Daily dose may vary based on INR, but strength must be confirmed. Confusion leads
to under- or overdosing.

fields.label: Suggested Fix
fields.text:
Specify tablet strength (e.g. “2 mg tab, 1 daily”)
If dose varies daily, write “see INR plan attached” and link it
Check that pharmacist/GP signs off on dose changes

fields.label: Common Error
fields.text:
Metformin XR prescribed, crushed, and administered without realising it’s extended-
release.

fields.label: Real Risk
fields.text:
Dose dumping, GI upset, reduced efficacy. Nurses may assume it’s safe due to lack of
“Do Not Crush” label.

fields.label: Suggested Fix
fields.text:
Don’t chart Metformin XR if resident has swallowing issues
Replace with Metformin IR (crushable)
Label as “Do Not Crush” in chart + MAR if kept
Update care plan and staff notes

fields.label: Common Error
fields.text:
Modified-release opioid (e.g. Targin, Oxycodone CR) crushed due to poor swallowing
or lack of clarity on formulation.

fields.label: Real Risk
fields.text: Overdose, respiratory depression, inconsistent pain control

fields.label: Suggested Fix
fields.text:
Chart as “Oxycodone IR” or oral liquid instead
Do not crush any CR opioid — use sticker/labelling
Re-chart clearly as “immediate-release” with administration note

entries.title: Tablets Crushed Without Any Care Plan Update

fields.label: Common Error
fields.text:
Resident begins having meds crushed, but no documentation in care plan, MAR, or
nursing notes.

fields.label: Real Risk
fields.text:
High-risk meds (e.g. enteric-coated, MR) crushed by default. New staff unaware of
change.

fields.label: Suggested Fix
fields.text:
Update care plan immediately when swallowing status changes
Use “Do Not Crush” labels where needed
Flag formulation switch (e.g. liquid or ODT used now)
Document photo/brand of med if needed for recognition

fields.label: Common Error
fields.text:
Oxazepam or risperidone PRN charted as “PRN” with no dose interval or max daily
frequency.

fields.label: Real Risk
fields.text:
Multiple doses given in 24 hours without oversight. No sedation monitoring or post-
dose documentation.

fields.label: Suggested Fix
fields.text:
Chart with specific frequency: “PRN up to 3×/day, minimum 6 hrs apart”
Add note: “Document reason + effect”
Include in pharmacist review if used >3×/week

fields.label: Common Error
fields.text:
Two PRN sedatives charted for agitation or behaviour with no escalation pathway or
usage hierarchy.

fields.label: Real Risk
fields.text: Both may be administered close together, increasing fall and restraint risk.

fields.label: Suggested Fix
fields.text:
Avoid concurrent sedative PRNs unless clearly justified
Use ONE PRN sedative with clear guidance
Document scenario for use: e.g. “Use if agitation escalates despite redirection”

entries.title: No PRN Charted for Pain, Despite Reported Discomfort

fields.label: Common Error
fields.text:
Resident reports pain intermittently but only has regular paracetamol or opioid — no
PRN option for flares.

fields.label: Real Risk
fields.text: Unmanaged pain, unnecessary behavioural escalation, or after-hours GP calls.

fields.label: Suggested Fix
fields.text:
Add PRN paracetamol or oral morphine liquid for known flares
Document when to offer PRN (e.g. “post-walk” or “at bedtime”)
Include PRN trial in MAC follow-up

Part 1 – Report Skeleton Templates
This section contains clean skeleton templates you can use when drafting clinical
reports. It includes frameworks for medication reviews, behaviour mapping,
psychotropic justification summaries, GP communication notes, progress-note
formats, and risk-summary layouts.
Each skeleton provides headings, subheadings, and sentence starters so you can
produce consistent, defensible documentation with minimal editing.
Part 2 – Clinical Reasoning and Decision Pathways
This section outlines how to structure your clinical reasoning when writing
recommendations.
It explains how to justify deprescribing, when to escalate to the GP, how to label
behaviours correctly, how to avoid restrictive-practice triggers in your wording, and
how to link each recommendation to diagnosis, indication, and symptom.
It provides guidance for avoiding ambiguous language, avoiding directive phrasing,
and ensuring that every suggestion is tied to a legitimate clinical rationale.
Part 3 – Approved TGA Indications and When Use Becomes Chemical Restraint
This section provides a medication-by-medication explanation of what the TGA has
officially approved.

entries.title: Why We Limit “Issue to Consider” to 1–2 Lines

fields.text:
•
Keeps the review focused and digestible for nurses and GPs
•
Avoids over-explaining — more detail goes into reasoning if needed
•
Supports bullet-style summaries in facility documentation or MAC reports
Example:
Issue: PRN risperidone used >3×/week with no charted effect

•
Avoids vague terms like “may benefit from” or “could consider”
•
Reduces ambiguity — helps GP know exactly what to do next
•
Demonstrates pharmacist accountability and clinical reasoning
Instead of:
“Consider switching to a safer formulation”
Use: “Switch to IR formulation and update chart with swallowing alert”

entries.title: Why Resident Name Is Omitted in Shared Report Examples

fields.text:
•
Maintains privacy in training tools
•
BUT: You should use the name in real-world submissions (e.g. “Mary may
benefit from…”)
•
Reinforces person-centred care when addressing behavioural issues
Report example:
“Mary has shown increased daytime sedation since regular quetiapine was
initiated…”

entries.title: Why Indications Are Always Included in the Medication Table

fields.text:
•
Prevents duplication (e.g. two antihypertensives, two sedatives)
•
Highlights polypharmacy without clear clinical reason
•
Identifies meds lacking ongoing benefit or current diagnosis

•
They’re often overlooked unless a pharmacist documents frequency
•
Falls, sedation, and chemical restraint audits often stem from PRN misuse
•
Easier to justify deprescribing if PRN hasn’t been used in weeks

•
Use Calibri or Arial, size 11–12
•
Align all tables and headings neatly — avoid mixed fonts
•
Maintain consistent margins and spacing
•
Use bold only for headings or section titles (e.g. Issue to Consider, Suggested
Action)

Good Example
Avoid
Single header row with clear lines
Multiple stacked rows
Horizontal spacing between columns Cramped or uneven cell widths
No colours or excessive shading
Red text, coloured cells, italics

•
Stick to 3–5 key actions per resident
•
Use appendices or supporting pages for full med lists if needed
•
Keep summaries short for MAC meetings (1–2 pages max)

This document integrates clinical best practice, deprescribing principles, and risk
monitoring across all medication domains relevant to aged-care residents.
Each section links to action-oriented recommendations designed to:
• Promote medication safety and rational prescribing.
• Support compliance with Aged Care Quality Standards 3 & 8.
• Align pharmacist, GP, and nursing review cycles under the facility’s Medication
Advisory Committee (MAC).
